Block 2

B2T1: Cluster/EMR

What you do: You launch an EMR cluster from the AWS console in your sandbox account, step by step, and check that it starts. You then terminate the cluster so that it stops billing.
Supports: L5 (Spark on a cluster) and A2, which runs its Spark job on EMR at two and then four core nodes.
Materials: step-by-step guide on Canvas.



B2T2: Spark/Glue
Two parts, each a Glue notebook in the B2T2 repository. Set up your account once with the repository’s step 1 before part A.
A Glue session bills until it stops, even after you close the browser tab. End each notebook with its last cell, %stop_session.

Part A: how Spark reads files

What you do: You run the notebook in your sandbox account and see, for each query, which folders, files and row groups Spark reads and how many tasks it starts. Exercises 2 to 6 then ask you to predict those numbers for new queries on the 36 months of taxi trips.
Supports: L7 (Spark as a managed service, and its demos on reading files).
Materials: the notebook l7a_data-read.ipynb.



Part B: slow queries and their fixes

What you do: You run three slow queries from L6 on Glue: input that can’t be split finely enough, a join on a hot key and a window query. Before each run you write down how many tasks you expect, then you read the stage table to find what makes the query slow and which change fixes it. Exercises B1 to B5 follow, with their answers in commented-out cells.
Supports: L6 (why a cluster job is slow) and L7.
Materials: the notebook l7b_slow-queries.ipynb.

Block 3

B3T1: Lakehouse/Athena+Glue

What you do: You query the course’s rides table in Athena, predicting how much each query reads before you run it. You then copy one month into your own account and change it: delete rows, read the table as it was before the delete, load a day twice and repair it, add a column, and join your copy with a course table.
Supports: L10 (lakehouses: Iceberg tables, snapshots and time travel) and L11, and the use and change tasks in A3.
Before the tutorial: run the one-time setup in the repository’s step 1 (in CloudShell).
Materials: the B3T1 repository: the steps, one SQL file per step with the expected results, and the setup script.



B3T2: Lakehouse/Glue build and maintain

What you do: You start a ready Glue job that loads one month of rides into an Iceberg table in your own account, and read its script while it runs. You predict how much a query will read from the table’s column sizes, then delete some rows, compact the table with OPTIMIZE, remove old snapshots and their files with VACUUM, and price the job’s run.
Supports: L10 and L11 (Iceberg maintenance: compaction, snapshots and VACUUM), and the build and maintain tasks in A3.
Before the tutorial: B3T1’s one-time setup, and the B2T2 setup, which creates your bucket and Glue role. Then run the repository’s step 2 in CloudShell.
Materials: the B3T2 repository: the steps, one SQL file per step with what to predict, the Glue job and the setup script.

title: L10 review: lakes, lakehouses and query engines
text:
Layers of a lakehouse

Which layer does each tool or format belong to?
In a lakehouse, your files stay in your own storage, and you pick a separate tool or format for each part that a cloud warehouse supplies as one service. Each tool or format below belongs to one of those parts.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Put each tool or format on its layer of a lakehouse. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Parquet :: Storage format
  > Parquet encodes the rows of one data file, column by column, with a footer. The table format (Iceberg) is the metadata above many such files.
- Spark :: Query engine
  > Spark SQL plans the query and runs the plan. On EMR, a cluster manager (YARN) starts Spark's executors on the cluster's nodes; YARN runs under the engine and is not a layer of the lakehouse.
- S3 :: Object storage
  > S3 stores data files and metadata files as objects; the table's metadata records which files form the table.
- Iceberg :: Table format
  > Iceberg's metadata files list the data files in the table's current snapshot, with the schema and the snapshots. Parquet encodes the rows.
- Trino :: Query engine
  > Trino plans the SQL query and runs the plan on its workers. A connector gives Trino access to one source, such as a data lake or a database, so it is part of the engine, not a layer of the lakehouse.
- Glue Data Catalog :: Catalog
  > The Glue Data Catalog lists tables and points each Iceberg table to its current metadata file.
- :: Cluster manager
  > A cluster manager (YARN on EMR, L5) starts Spark's executors on the nodes. It runs under the engine and is not one of the lakehouse's parts.
- :: Connector
  > In Trino a connector is how the engine reads one source, for example the Glue Data Catalog (L10). It belongs to the engine, not to a layer of its own.

title: L10 review: lakes, lakehouses and query engines
text:
What the lakehouse changes

Data lake, lakehouse, or both?
An online shop’s orders, kept two ways. In the data lake, the table is a folder of Parquet files in S3, one subfolder per day. In the lakehouse, the table is an Iceberg table in the Glue Data Catalog over those Parquet files, partitioned by the day of order_time. Athena reads both tables and changes the Iceberg table.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Does each statement describe the data lake, the lakehouse, or both? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The rows are stored as Parquet objects in an S3 bucket :: Both
  > Both keep Parquet files in S3. The difference is the table format and the catalog above them.
- A query skips day folders only if its filter uses the folder partition column :: Data lake
  > In a data lake the engine can skip day folders only when the filter uses the folder partition column (P2). An Iceberg table's partition value is derived from the order time (Iceberg partitioning), so a filter on the order time skips other days.
- A delete adds a small file that lists the removed rows, and the data file is not changed :: Lakehouse
  > Iceberg calls it a delete file, and Athena's `DELETE` on an Iceberg table writes one (P4). Readers skip the rows it lists, and the data file itself is not changed. A folder of Parquet files has no delete files: changing a row means writing a new copy of its file.
- A query can read the table as it was last Friday, while that snapshot is still retained :: Lakehouse
  > Iceberg keeps each snapshot until it is expired, and time travel reads an earlier one (P5). A folder has no snapshots, so nothing records which files formed the table last Friday.
- A data file is not edited after it is written :: Both
  > In both, a Parquet file is never edited once written. The lakehouse adds delete files or new data files instead (P4).
- A reader lists the folder and reads whatever files are there now :: Data lake
  > A folder has no table commit that makes all files of one write visible together, so a reader can see part of a write (P1). An Iceberg reader finds the data files through the current snapshot's manifests instead of listing the folder.
- :: Neither
  > Every statement here describes the data lake, the lakehouse, or both of them.

title: L10 review: lakes, lakehouses and query engines
text:
Terms used on this page

Lake and lakehouse
Data lake. Raw files in object storage, read by engines that list the folders; a folder of files has no commit, no record of its schema and no history.
Lakehouse. A lake whose tables have a table format and a catalog, so readers see whole commits.
Query engine. Parses SQL, plans it and runs it: Spark SQL, Trino, DuckDB, Athena.
Catalog. Lists tables and points to each table’s current metadata file: the Glue Data Catalog.
Table format. Metadata files that say which data files are the table now, with the schema and the snapshots: Iceberg.
Object storage. Keeps files as objects in buckets: S3. Which files form a table is recorded in the metadata above it.
Storage format (file format). Encodes rows in one data file, with a footer: Parquet.


Iceberg’s levels
Catalog entry. The table’s name and the path of its current metadata file.
Metadata file. The schema, the partition spec (how files are grouped, for example by month) and the snapshots; each snapshot names a manifest list.
Manifest. Lists data files, each with its partition value, row count, and minimum and maximum per column.
Data file. A file that contains rows of a table: a Parquet file.
Commit. Writing new metadata files, then switching the catalog entry to the new one in one step; readers see the old snapshot or the new one, never half.
Snapshot. One version of the table: the data files that were the table after one commit.


What the table format fixes
Iceberg partitioning. The table is partitioned by a value Iceberg derives from a column, for example the month of pickup_datetime, and each data file’s partition value is kept in the manifests. Because the value is derived (hidden partitioning), a filter on the column itself skips files, with no folder partition column to name. Separately, the manifests keep each file’s minimum and maximum per column, which also let an engine skip files.
Delete file. A small file that lists which rows of a data file are deleted. Readers skip those rows, and the data file itself is not changed.
Compaction. Rewriting many small data files into fewer larger ones (OPTIMIZE).
Time travel. Reading the table as it was at an earlier snapshot, as long as that snapshot has not been expired.


Not layers of a lakehouse
Cluster manager. Starts an engine’s processes on a cluster’s nodes, for example YARN starting Spark’s executors on EMR (L5).
Connector. In Trino, how the engine reads one source, such as the Glue Data Catalog or a database (L10).
_SUCCESS file. An empty file Spark writes when a job finishes writing a folder; readers of the folder do not check it by default.
Folder partition column. A column whose value is a folder name, such as month=2024-03; a data lake skips folders only when a query names it.

Block 1: lectures 1 to 3

1. Who is responsible: AWS or you

---

---

## In which service is **AWS** responsible for each of these? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The hardware: the racks and the power :: Both
    > AWS is responsible for the hardware under both: the racks and the power under an instance and under a function. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- The virtual machine layer the code runs on :: Both
    > AWS is responsible for the virtual machine layer under both. An instance is a virtual machine on AWS's hardware; for a function, AWS starts a small virtual machine to hold its execution environment. Where to look: L2 slide 20; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- Starting more copies of the code when many calls arrive at once :: Lambda
    > On a function, AWS is responsible for the capacity: AWS starts more execution environments as calls arrive. On an instance, the capacity is your responsibility: you choose the instance type and start more instances yourself. Where to look: L3 slide 23 and L2 slide 20; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- Patching the language runtime the code uses :: Lambda
    > On a function, you pick a runtime version from AWS's list, and AWS is responsible for patching it. On an instance, you install the runtime, so patching it is your responsibility. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- Checking that the code gives the right answer :: Neither
    > Testing the code is your responsibility, both on an instance and on a function. AWS runs the code but is not responsible for what the code computes. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- The policy that says what your code may touch :: Neither
    > You write the policy, both on an instance and on a function: a role on an instance, an execution role on a function. AWS enforces the policy on both, but is not responsible for writing it. Where to look: L2 slide 30; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).
- :: EC2
    > On a function, AWS is responsible for everything it is responsible for on an instance, and for more. AWS is responsible for the bottom two bands on EC2, and for those two plus three more on Lambda. Where to look: L2 slide 20 and L3 slide 23; practise [Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-who-handles-each-task).



2. Stop or terminate

---

---

## An EC2 instance was launched with its own volume, left on the default of being deleted when the instance is terminated. A second volume was attached later to hold the data, and that one was set to be kept when the instance is terminated. Each volume is billed for its full size while it exists, whether or not the space is used. Which condition does each description below fit? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Both volumes are there, and the per-second compute charge is being paid :: Running instance
    > AWS charges for a running instance's compute by the second and for both volumes' space: nothing has been switched off. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- Both volumes are there and charged for, and no compute charge is being paid :: Stopped instance
    > Stopping ends the compute charge and keeps both volumes, and AWS still charges for their space. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The launch volume and everything installed on it are kept for the next start, and the compute bill has stopped :: Stopped instance
    > Stopping ends the compute charge and keeps both volumes, and AWS still charges for their storage, so the data and software stay for the next start. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The launch volume is gone, and only the volume attached later is still charged for :: Terminated instance
    > Terminating deleted the launch volume because it was set to be deleted. The attached volume was set to be kept, so it remains after termination and AWS still charges for its storage. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The launch volume no longer exists, and neither does what was installed on it :: Terminated instance
    > Terminating deleted the launch volume, which was left on its default of being deleted, along with everything installed on it. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- Somebody is logged in right now, and compute is charged by the second :: Running instance
    > AWS charges for a running instance's compute by the second and for both volumes' storage, whether or not anyone is using the instance. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- :: Instance never launched
    > Every description here is of an instance that was launched with these volumes and is now running, stopped or terminated. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 38; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).



3. Launch settings for a notebook instance *

## You launch one EC2 instance to explore a dataset in a Jupyter notebook. The data is 10 GB in a compressed Parquet file in S3. Which launch setting settles each requirement below? Not all options will be used.

- Python 3.12 and the AWS CLI must already be in place the first time the instance boots: no install commands may run at all, not even at first boot :: Image
    > The image is what the instance starts from: its operating system and the software already on it. A user data script could install Python at first boot, but the requirement rules out running any install commands. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- Loaded into pandas, the file takes about 30 GB of memory, and the whole DataFrame must fit in memory at once :: Instance type
    > The type fixes memory, cores and network. Disk space doesn't help: a DataFrame is held in memory, and the file itself stays in S3. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- AWS lets connections reach the instance only on port 8888, and only from your own IP address :: Security group
    > A security group decides which ports are reachable from which addresses. A security group does not check who you are or decide what the instance may read in S3. Where to look: L2 slides 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- The notebook reads the file from S3 without anyone putting access keys in a file on the instance :: Role
    > An EC2 instance can be given a role. The role's policy says what the instance may read, so no one has to paste access keys into a file on the instance. Where to look: L2 slides 25 and 29–30; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- :: User data script
    > Commands the instance runs at first boot. Here everything needed is either in the image or set by another setting. Where to look: L2 slide 25; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).
- :: Volume size
    > Volume size sets disk space, not memory, and the file is read from S3, not stored on the disk. Where to look: L2 slide 27; practise [Setting up an instance for the harvest records](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l2.html#q-setting-up-an-instance-for-the-harvest-records).



4. A function or an instance

---

---

## Which fits each piece of work best? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A file of a few MB lands in an S3 bucket a few times an hour and needs a few seconds of work to convert :: Function
    > Each file's arrival is an event that starts a few seconds of work, and there is nothing to do between arrivals. No compute is used or billed between calls. Where to look: L3 slides 5, 13 and 39; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A model fit on a 2 GB table that takes forty minutes, cannot be broken into shorter steps, and runs once a night :: EC2 instance
    > A function call stops after fifteen minutes, and the model fit cannot be split into shorter calls. An instance can run the model fit and then stop, and its memory can hold the table. Where to look: L3 slide 13; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- Someone working in a notebook all afternoon on a 5 GB table, changing code and re-running it :: EC2 instance
    > The session has to keep running between keystrokes, and the data has to stay in memory from one cell to the next. Saving files between calls keeps the files but not the session. Where to look: L3 slide 5 and L2 slide 19; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A web endpoint answering a few short requests a minute, at all hours, where a second's delay now and then is fine :: Function
    > Each request starts a short call, and there is nothing to do between requests. No compute is used or billed between calls. Where to look: L3 slides 5, 13 and 39; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- A daily summary of yesterday's 200 MB that takes two minutes and writes one file :: Function
    > A schedule starts two minutes of work once a day, and there is nothing to do between runs. No compute is used or billed between calls. Where to look: L3 slides 5, 13 and 39; practise [Function, split calls or an instance for each workload](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-function-split-calls-or-an-instance-for-each-workload).
- :: Cluster of several nodes
    > Every workload here fits on one instance, in its memory and in its time. Several nodes help only when one instance cannot handle the work. Where to look: L4 slides 9–10; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).



5. What starts the function

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A smart-home company runs several functions. What starts the function in each situation below? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Someone asks the voice assistant "what is the temperature?" and it answers a second later :: Request
    > Someone is waiting for the reply: a request starts the function and gets the answer back. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- A thermostat writes a new reading file to a bucket, and a function checks whether the reading is outside the safe range :: Event
    > The new file's arrival is the event; a rule sends that event to the function. Nobody waits for the check. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- A new firmware file is uploaded to a bucket, and a function checks its signature :: Event
    > The upload is the event; a rule sends that event to the function. Nobody waits for the result. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- A new recording from a door camera lands in a bucket, and a function blurs the faces in it :: Event
    > The recording's arrival is the event; a rule sends that event to the function. Nobody waits for the result. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- Every night at 03:00 a function deletes test devices' logs older than a week :: Schedule
    > A schedule starts the function at a clock time: 03:00 every night. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- On the first day of each month a function totals each household's energy use :: Schedule
    > A schedule starts the function on a calendar date: the first day of each month. Where to look: L3 slides 5 and 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).
- :: Deployment
    > Deploying a new version stores the new code for later calls. Deploying does not call the handler; the handler runs only when a request, an event or a schedule starts the function. Where to look: L2 slide 36 and L3 slides 5, 8–9; practise [Requests, events and schedules](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l3.html#q-requests-events-and-schedules).



6. Why the Parquet read is small

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A weather service keeps five years of hourly station readings in S3 as one Parquet file: 9.6 GB, 22 columns of about the same size, sorted by reading time, in 120 row groups of about the same size. A query asks for the average wind speed per station in the first week of July 2024, which needs that week and 3 of the 22 columns. Run with DuckDB, it reads about 20 MB from S3. Which reading explains 20 MB?

1. [x] Needed columns only, from row groups that can contain the week
    > Both savings at once. One week's rows are in 1 or 2 of the 120 row groups (each about 80 MB with all columns), and only 3 of 22 columns are read from them: about 11 to 22 MB. The footer's minimum and maximum reading time per row group say which row groups can hold that week. Where to look: L1 slides 13–14 and L4 slide 15; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
1. [ ] Only 3 of the 22 columns are read, but from every row group in the file
    > Skipping columns alone would read 3/22 of 9.6 GB, about 1.3 GB. The row groups outside that week are skipped too, from the footer's minimum and maximum. Where to look: L1 slides 13–14; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
1. [ ] Only the row groups that can hold that week are read, but with all 22 columns
    > Skipping row groups alone would read 1 or 2 row groups with every column, about 80 to 160 MB. Each column's bytes are stored apart, so the 19 unneeded columns are skipped too. Where to look: L1 slide 13 and L4 slide 15; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).
1. [ ] Footer stores a copy of the needed rows, so no data pages are read
    > The footer holds metadata: where each column chunk of each row group is stored, and each chunk's minimum and maximum. The rows themselves are read from the data pages the footer points to. Where to look: L4 slide 15; practise [May 2025 downloads: reading the file over the network](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l1.html#q-how-much-data-does-the-may-2025-query-fetch).



7. Where the S3 client is made

---

## A scooter-share company keeps its trips as Parquet in S3, in one folder for each trip date: `trip_date=2025-07-01/`, `trip_date=2025-07-02/`, and so on. The fleet has scooters SC-0001 to SC-2000. Each folder holds one file, sorted by scooter id, with about 10 row groups. Each file's footer records the minimum and maximum of each column in each row group, and Spark can use them. Which data can Spark skip for each condition? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-14' AND scooter_id = 'SC-0417'` :: Whole folders and row groups
    > The date names one folder, so the others are skipped. Inside that day's file, sorted by scooter id, the footers rule out the row groups that cannot hold SC-0417. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE trip_date IN ('2025-07-14', '2025-07-15')` :: Whole folders
    > Two folders match by name, and all the others are skipped. Every row in the two matching folders is needed. Where to look: L4 slides 21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE scooter_id BETWEEN 'SC-0400' AND 'SC-0499'` :: Only row groups inside the files
    > The condition does not name the folder column, so every day's folder is opened. Each file is sorted by scooter id, so the footers rule out the row groups outside that range. Where to look: L4 slides 21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE scooter_id = 'SC-0417' AND battery_end < 10`. Every row group has some trips that ended below 10% battery :: Only row groups inside the files
    > The condition does not name the folder column, so every day's folder is opened. Each file is sorted by scooter id, so the footers rule out the row groups that cannot hold SC-0417; the battery condition rules out nothing. Where to look: L4 slide 20; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-14' AND battery_end < 10`. Every row group has some trips that ended below 10% battery :: Whole folders
    > The date skips the other folders. Inside that day's file the battery condition rules out no row group. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- `WHERE trip_date = '2025-07-20' AND scooter_id BETWEEN 'SC-0100' AND 'SC-0199'` :: Whole folders and row groups
    > The date names one folder, so the others are skipped. Inside that day's file, sorted by scooter id, the footers rule out the row groups outside that range. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).
- :: Neither folders nor row groups
    > Spark skips a folder when the condition names the folder column, and a row group when the footer's minimum and maximum rule it out. A condition on the date or on the scooter id always skips something here. Where to look: L4 slides 20–21 and 23; practise [What does each filter condition make Spark read?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-what-does-each-filter-condition-make-spark-read).

## In a PySpark notebook on an EMR cluster, `recent` is a Spark DataFrame of 2025's ticket sales made from Parquet files in S3, `venues_pd` is a pandas DataFrame, `pd` is pandas, and `F` is `pyspark.sql.functions`. - `venues_pd = pd.read_parquet("s3://tickets-raw/venues.parquet")` :: pandas does the work in the driver only, with no Spark plan

## A PySpark notebook on an EMR cluster reads a month of parcel scans, stored as 30 daily Parquet files, and writes each depot's totals as Parquet. The cluster is terminated at the end of the day. Where is each thing below kept while the notebook runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The 300 depot totals, turned into a pandas DataFrame with toPandas() to draw a chart in the notebook :: In the memory of the driver
    > A pandas DataFrame is held in the driver's process: toPandas() brings the 300 rows there from the executors. Where to look: L5 slides 24–25; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A small list of depot names read with pd.read_csv in the notebook :: In the memory of the driver

Where to look: L5 slides 32–33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A public Parquet dataset that several teams' clusters read :: In an S3 bucket

Where to look: L5 slides 31 and 33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).
- A results file a teammate opens next week, after this cluster is terminated :: In an S3 bucket
    > S3 keeps the results file after the cluster is terminated, while the cluster's disks are lost, so a teammate can open the file next week. Where to look: L5 slides 31 and 33; practise [Where is each piece of data kept?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-where-is-each-piece-of-data-kept).

## A 230 MB Parquet file holds 6 row groups of about the same size. The cluster grows from 8 slots to 16, and Spark's scan of the file now makes 16 tasks. How many of those tasks read rows?

1. [x] 6
    > Spark cuts the file into about 16 byte ranges, and each row group is read whole by the one range that holds its middle. The 6 middles fall in 6 different ranges, so 6 tasks read rows and 10 read none. Where to look: L6 slides 28–29 and 20.
1. [ ] 16
    > Every task gets a byte range, but a range that holds no row group's middle reads no rows. A row group is never split between tasks and never read twice. Where to look: L6 slide 28.
1. [ ] 12
    > A row group is never split between tasks: the one task whose range holds its middle reads all of it. Each of the 6 row groups is read by one task, not by two. Where to look: L6 slide 28.
1. [ ] 1
    > A file with a single row group gives one task that reads rows. Here the 6 row groups have 6 middles, spread across the file. Where to look: L6 slides 20 and 29.



15. Nodes for a deadline
A mapping company must render 1,800 satellite image tiles on an EMR cluster before the morning. The tiles are independent of each other, and each takes 6 minutes on one vCPU. They can be spread over any number of vCPUs with no overhead. The cluster has one primary node, which renders nothing, plus core nodes of type m6a.xlarge, each with 4 vCPUs for rendering. Launch takes 15 minutes before the first tile can start, and everything must finish 3 hours after the cluster starts, launch included.
This scenario has two questions. After you answer the first, click → to go to the second.

## Step 1: how much work is it, in vCPU-hours (core-hours)?

1. [ ] 10,800
    > 10,800 is the work in vCPU-minutes. 10,800 divided by 60 is 180 vCPU-hours. Where to look: L4 slide 35; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [x] 180
    > 1,800 tiles × 6 minutes is 10,800 vCPU-minutes, which is 180 vCPU-hours. L4 also says core-hours, the same count in allocated CPU cores. Where to look: L4 slides 35–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither), [How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l5.html#q-how-many-tasks-can-this-cluster-run-at-once).
1. [ ] 1,800
    > 1,800 is the number of tiles. Each tile takes 6 minutes of one vCPU's work. Where to look: L4 slide 35; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [ ] 45
    > 45 is node-hours: 180 divided by a node's 4 vCPUs. The work itself is 180 vCPU-hours. Where to look: L4 slide 37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).

## Step 2: what is the smallest number of core nodes that finishes in time?

1. [ ] 15
    > 15 nodes ignores the launch: 180 vCPU-hours over the full 3 hours is 60 vCPUs, but only 2 hours 45 minutes are left for rendering. Where to look: L4 slides 36–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).
1. [ ] 16
    > Sixteen nodes give 64 vCPUs. 180 vCPU-hours spread over 64 vCPUs takes about 2 hours 49 minutes, more than the 2 hours 45 minutes left after the launch. Where to look: L4 slides 36–37; practise [Scale up, scale out, or neither?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/l4.html#q-scale-up-scale-out-or-neither).

The shop has 50,000 customers with about 40 orders each, and one reseller account placed 2 million orders. After the `Exchange` by customer, one task takes 25 seconds and the median task 0.2 seconds. Select every statement that is true.

- [ ] For the running-total window, each task before the `Exchange` replaces its reseller rows with one partial total
    > False. The window produces a running total for every order, so Spark must keep and move the reseller's individual rows. Partial totals are enough for a count or sum per customer, but not for a running total. Where to look: L6 slides 31 and 40; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).

    > False. The window groups rows by customer (`Window.partitionBy`). After the `Exchange`, one task still receives all of the reseller's orders, whether or not they were sorted by date before. Where to look: L6 slides 39–40; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).
- [x] A different job that only counts orders per customer sends partial counts through the `Exchange`, not every order
    > True. For a count per customer, each task before the `Exchange` produces one partial count for each customer in that task's input. The `Exchange` moves those partial counts instead of all 2 million reseller orders. For the running total in this shop's job, Spark moves every order. - [ ] An `Exchange` by customer spreads the reseller's orders evenly across the tasks of the next stage
    > False. An `Exchange` by customer sends every row with the same customer to the same task in the next stage. Spreading the reseller's orders evenly would break the grouping by customer that the window needs. Where to look: L6 slides 30 and 39; practise [Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?](https://cpsc436c-2026w1.github.io/lecture-reviews/w2-l6.html#q-diagnostics-questions).

title: Midterm review
text:
Terms used on this page
The vocabulary of lectures 1 to 7, grouped as on the flashcards: practise the flashcards and the matching set.

Compute and billing
Instance (EC2). A virtual machine you rent from AWS, billed per second for the time it runs. Stopping it ends the compute charge, but its EBS disk still bills.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
Spot instance. Spare EC2 capacity sold much cheaper than on-demand. AWS can take it back after a two-minute warning, so it suits work that can stop and restart.
Provisioned capacity. Compute you pay for while it is allocated to you, used or not. Unlike pay-per-use compute, its charge continues when nothing runs.
Usage-based billing. Charges for measured work, such as each request or each millisecond a function runs. They stop when nothing runs; stored data and logs still cost money.
Idle test. The question to ask of each compute charge: does it bill while nothing runs? If yes, it is provisioned capacity. Storage and logs are counted separately.
Time shape of demand. When a workload asks for its resources across a day or a week: a steady rate, a daily rhythm, a burst, or a scheduled job. With the peak rate, it decides whether provisioned or usage-based billing is cheaper.
Cost granularity. The unit a provider bills in, such as one second of instance time or one request. With per-second billing, a faster, pricier instance can come out cheaper per task.
Ephemeral infrastructure. A server or cluster created for one piece of work and deleted after it, so it bills only around that work. Our EMR clusters were launched for a run and terminated after.


Storage and access
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.
Bucket. A named container in S3 that holds objects. Its name is part of every object’s address.
Object key. The full name of one stored file inside an S3 bucket. It is only a name, unrelated to the column a group-by or a join uses.
Prefix (S3). The leading part of an object’s name, such as day=2012-06-14/. S3 lists objects by it, and the console’s folders are built from it; the general-purpose buckets we use have no real folders.
EBS volume. A disk an EC2 instance reaches over the network, as its main disk or an extra one. Its data survives a stop, and it bills per GB-month while it exists, even when the instance is stopped.
Byte-range read. Asking S3 for one stated part of an object instead of the whole object. Parquet libraries fetch the footer this way, then only the column chunks a query needs.
IAM policy. A JSON document that says which actions are allowed on which AWS resources. Attached to a role, it sets what anything using that role may do.
Security group. The rules that say what network traffic may reach an EC2 instance and what it may send out, by protocol, port and address. They do not decide what the instance may do with other AWS resources.


Serverless functions
Serverless. A service model where the platform runs and scales your code and you never pick or patch the computers under it. It usually bills per request and running time; stored data still costs money.
Lambda function. The unit you deploy to AWS Lambda: your code and its settings, run each time a trigger fires. One setting, memory, also sets its CPU and its price per millisecond.
Execution role. The identity AWS takes on when it runs a Lambda function. It decides which resources the code may read or change.
Execution environment. The isolated space AWS sets up to run a Lambda function, with its memory and a temporary disk. AWS may reuse it for later calls and pauses it between them.
Cold start. The set-up before the first call in a new Lambda environment: AWS loads the code, then your code’s initialisation runs, such as opening connections and importing libraries.
Handler. The function in your code that Lambda calls on each invocation, taking event and context. Code outside it runs once per environment, so a client built there is reused.
Request (trigger). A call that asks a Lambda function for an answer while the caller waits for it, such as a browser going through API Gateway.
Event (trigger). A report that something happened, such as a new object landing in a bucket. A Lambda function processes it with no caller waiting for an answer.
EventBridge. The AWS service whose rules match things that happen, such as a new object in a bucket, or fire on a clock, and send each match to a target such as a Lambda function.
API Gateway. The AWS service that gives a function a web address, so a browser or a program can call it over HTTP. Its simplest kind waits at most 30 seconds for an answer.


Files, memory and layout
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Row group. A horizontal block inside one Parquet file, holding one column chunk per column. Its size is set when the file is written, and a file can hold one or many.
Column chunk. The values of one field within one row group of a Parquet file. The writer can store their min and max, which lets a reader skip the whole row group.
Footer (Parquet). The metadata at the end of a Parquet file: the schema, where each column chunk starts and, if the writer stored them, each chunk’s min and max. A reader fetches it before any data.
Projection pushdown. Handing the reader the list of columns a query uses, so it reads only those columns from a Parquet file.
Predicate pushdown. Handing the reader the query’s filter, so it can skip row groups whose stored min and max show that no row can match.
Folder partition. A dataset layout with one named location per value of a column, such as day=2012-06-14/ (on S3, a prefix). A filter on that column skips the other locations without opening them.
Compaction. Rewriting many small files into fewer, larger ones, so a query opens fewer files. Too few files, or too few row groups, can leave cores idle.
Eager load. Reading the whole dataset into memory before the work starts. If data and working space exceed memory, the operating system swaps to disk or stops the program.
Storage, memory, compute and network. The four things every data task uses, each with a capacity and a rate. Looking at a job from each in turn helps find its bottleneck, and cloud architecture often trades one for another.


Spark: how a job runs
Driver. The program that coordinates a Spark application: it runs your code, builds the query plan and sends tasks to the executors.
Executor. A Spark program running on an EMR core or task node. It runs tasks and keeps their data in its memory or on the node’s disk.
Partition. A chunk of rows that one task processes as one unit. When reading files it holds one or more splits, each a byte range of one file, planned from the file sizes and the number of slots.
Task. One stage’s work on one chunk of rows, run in one slot: by default, one executor core.
Slot. One executor core, as room to run one task on one Spark partition at a time. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks at once; our EMR nodes have one per vCPU.
Stage. A set of tasks Spark can run before rows have to move between partitions. Every task in it runs the same steps on a different partition.
Wave. The set of a stage’s tasks that run at the same time, one per slot. 36 reading tasks on 8 slots need 5 of them.
Transformation. A step such as filter or groupBy(...).count() that is only recorded in the plan. No task runs until an action asks for a result.
Action. On a Spark DataFrame, a call such as df.count(), df.collect() or df.write.parquet() that makes Spark run the plan built so far. Unlike pandas, where each step runs as soon as you call it.


Spark: shuffles and slow stages
Narrow transformation. A step each task does on its own partition, so no rows move between partitions: filter, select, withColumn.
Wide transformation. A step that needs rows from other partitions, such as groupBy, orderBy, a window or most joins. Spark adds a shuffle before it.
Shuffle (Exchange). Moving rows between partitions for the next stage: each task writes its rows to its node’s disk, and the next stage’s tasks read them, often from other nodes.
Window query. A step that computes a value over a group of rows and puts it on each row, such as each trip’s payment-type average next to the trip. Every row goes into an Exchange.
Hot key. One join, window or sort value with far more rows than the others. All its rows go to one task, which runs long after the rest of its stage; more nodes do not help.
Spill. Writing to the node’s disk when the rows a task sorts, groups or shuffles do not fit in its share of executor memory. The result is correct but slower.


Clusters and managed Spark
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node (EMR). The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node (EMR). An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node (EMR). An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing HDFS data.
HDFS. A file system that splits files into blocks across a cluster’s core nodes’ disks. Its data is lost when the cluster terminates, so our inputs and outputs stay on S3.
AWS Glue. AWS’s managed Spark service with a visual job editor and table definitions: you choose a job’s worker type and number of workers, or let it scale them, and it starts the workers. A notebook session bills until you stop it, and its idle timeout is 48 hours by default.
Worker type (Glue). The size of each Glue worker, from G.1X (1 DPU: 4 vCPU, 16 GB) upward, such as G.2X at 2 DPUs. Together with the number of workers it defines a job’s capacity, while the service picks the hardware underneath.
DPU (Glue). Glue’s billing unit: 4 vCPU and 16 GB, the size of one G.1X worker, billed per second, with a 1-minute minimum, while a job runs or a session exists.

text:
How Spark runs our query

Where does each step of the query run?
The lecture’s example data are the New York City yellow taxi trips from 2011 to 2013, about 520 million trips in 36 monthly Parquet files on S3. An EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge, runs the query from L5: the rides and the average total per payment type for June 2012. Each core node has one executor with 4 cores, so the cluster has 8 slots.
by_pay = (spark.read.parquet("s3://…/taxi/parquet/")
  .filter((F.col("tpep_pickup_datetime") >= "2012-06-01")
        & (F.col("tpep_pickup_datetime") <  "2012-07-01"))
  .groupBy("payment_type")
  .agg(F.count("*").alias("rides"),
       F.avg("total_amount").alias("avg_total")))
by_pay.collect()

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each step of the June 2012 query, where does it run? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- read the trip rows from the files: `spark.read.parquet` / `FROM` :: task, on its own Spark partition, before any Exchange
    > Each task reads its own Spark partition, without rows from any other Spark partition. The Spark partition is a set of byte ranges of the files. The task reads every row of each row group whose middle falls in one of its ranges, and only the needed columns. A task whose ranges hold no row group's middle reads no rows: 16 of the 52 tasks here.
- keep only the trips for June 2012: `filter` / `WHERE` :: task, on its own Spark partition, before any Exchange
    > Each task filters its own Spark partition, without rows from any other Spark partition: it keeps or drops each row it holds.
- drop the columns no longer needed (Spark adds this step itself) :: task, on its own Spark partition, before any Exchange
    > Each task drops the columns on its own Spark partition, without rows from any other Spark partition: it keeps only `payment_type` and `total_amount` on the rows it already holds. Reading only the needed columns happened earlier, in the scan.
- finish the count and average per payment type: `groupBy().agg()` / `GROUP BY` :: task, after the `Exchange`
    > A task can total its own rows, but Spark plans the step before it knows where the rows are, and a payment type's rows can be in any Spark partition. So the partial totals go into an `Exchange` first, even in the measured run, where one task held every June 2012 trip. "Driver" is wrong here: the driver never adds up trip rows. The stage-2 task also works on one Spark partition, but the `Exchange` fills that partition with partial rows from every stage-1 task, so the step cannot run before an `Exchange`.
- return the answer to your program: `collect()` :: driver
    > `collect()` returns the 5 final rows to the driver, the process that runs your program.
- :: YARN, on the primary node
    > Picking YARN confuses the cluster manager with the process that runs the query steps. YARN starts each executor on a core node with enough free memory and runs no step of the query; the cores per executor are a Spark setting. The query's steps run in the executors, and the driver plans them.

section: From code to a physical plan
text:
From code to a physical plan

Self-check: what does an Exchange do?
In the measured run of the June 2012 query on the 2 core nodes, stage 1 reads the 36 monthly files and computes partial totals, and stage 2 finishes the count and average per payment type. An Exchange (shuffle) separates the two stages. These are the measurements around the Exchange:
stage 1, scan       52 tasks on core nodes 1 and 2;
                    1 task, on node 1, had June 2012 trips
partial rows        5 from that task, one per payment type, 367 B in all
stage 2, planned    1000 shuffle partitions (EMR's default)
stage 2, ran        1 task, on core node 2:
                    adaptive execution merged the 1000 into 1
result              5 rows, to the driver

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## In the June 2012 run, what moves over the network in the `Exchange` (shuffle)?

1. [ ] Input files, read again from S3
    > Picking the input files treats the `Exchange` as a second scan. Stage 2 reads what stage 1 wrote, here 5 partial rows; the input files are read once, by stage 1.
1. [ ] Every June 2012 trip the scan kept
    > Picking every trip skips the partial totals. Stage 1 already added up its June 2012 trips into one row per payment type, so only those 5 rows go into the `Exchange`.
1. [x] Rows for a task on another node
    > The task on node 1 wrote 5 rows for the stage-2 task on node 2, so those 367 B went over the network. If the stage-2 task had run on node 1, those rows would not have crossed the network.

## In the June 2012 run, when could the stage-2 task start? \*

1. [ ] As soon as the task with the June 2012 trips had written its 5 rows
    > Starting stage 2 after the one task with June 2012 trips assumes Spark knows where the rows are. Spark cannot know that the other 51 tasks will add nothing until they finish, so every task of stage 1 must end first.
1. [x] Once the last of the 52 stage-1 tasks had finished
    > Stage 2 needs the partial rows from all of stage 1, so the `Exchange` is a stage boundary: the one stage-2 task started after the last scan task finished, although only one of the 52 tasks had rows for it.
1. [ ] As soon as the driver had built the plan
    > Starting stage 2 when the driver builds the plan confuses building the plan with producing data. The driver builds the plan before tasks run, but stage 2 must wait until the stage-1 tasks produce their rows.

## Spark planned 1000 shuffle partitions for stage 2 of the June 2012 query. What decides which of them gets a row?

1. [ ] Node that wrote the row
    > Picking the node expects rows to stay where they were written. A row can go to a task on any node; here the rows from node 1 went to a task on node 2.
1. [x] Row's key, its payment type
    > All rows with the same payment type go to the same shuffle partition. The plan's `hashpartitioning(payment_type, …)` hashes the key to choose that partition, so one task can finish the payment type's totals.
1. [ ] Order in which rows were read
    > Assigning rows by read order would split one payment type across several tasks. Rows with the same key must go to the same shuffle partition regardless of read order.

## In the June 2012 run, where were the 5 partial rows stored between stage 1 and stage 2?

1. [x] On node 1's disk
    > The stage-1 task on node 1 wrote its 5 rows to a shuffle file on node 1's disk, and the stage-2 task on node 2 fetched them from there over the network.
1. [ ] In S3, next to the input files
    > Picking S3 treats the `Exchange` as a write to storage outside the cluster. S3 holds the query's input files, which stage 1 reads once; rows between stages stay on the nodes' disks.
1. [ ] In the driver's memory
    > Picking the driver assumes the driver receives and passes on the partial rows. The driver plans the stages and receives only the 5 result rows from `collect()`; the stage-2 task fetched the partial rows from node 1 directly.

## A teammate wants to shorten the June 2012 query and starts with the group-by, because it is the one step that needs rows from other nodes. Which part of the run should a change target first?

1. [ ] Stage 2: group totals
    > Picking stage 2 assumes the group-by takes most of the time. Stage 2 ran one task for 0.011 s, because it added up only 5 partial rows.
1. [ ] `Exchange` between the stages
    > Picking the `Exchange` expects moving data between nodes to cost most. The `Exchange` received 5 rows, 367 B, and stage 2 waited 0 ms to fetch them.
1. [x] Stage 1: scan
    > Stage 1 took 8.58 s of the 8.90 s query, and stage 2 took 0.011 s: reading the 36 files took most of the time. The stage's *Duration* field shows the 8.58 s.

Slide: 22 (also 19)


What sets the time of stage 1?
Stage 1 of the June 2012 query reads the 36 monthly files of taxi trips, keeps the June 2012 trips and computes partial totals. Stage 1 uses 2 core nodes, each with one executor of 4 cores; each executor core is a slot, which runs one task at a time. Spark cut the files into 52 Spark partitions, one task each:
tasks that read rows     36, about 1.65 s each (9 in 10 at 1.75 s or less)
tasks that read nothing  16, under 0.1 s each
slots                    2 executors × 4 cores = 8
stage time               8.58 s
The tasks that run at the same time, one per slot, form a wave (a term from Hadoop). The Spark UI’s event timeline shows each wave as a column of task bars; the UI does not use the term wave.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Each slot runs one task at a time. What sets how long stage 1 takes on the 8 slots?

1. [ ] Total work split evenly over 8 slots
    > Dividing the total work by 8 assumes the work can be split evenly: 36 × 1.65 s ÷ 8 is about 7.4 s. Each task runs as a whole in one slot, so the 36 tasks cannot be spread evenly over 8 slots.
1. [ ] Slowest single task
    > The slowest task sets the stage time only when one task is much slower than the rest. Here each reading task takes about 1.65 s, and the 8.58 s stage time is about five task times one after another.
1. [x] Number of waves of tasks
    > The 36 tasks that read rows run in 4 waves of 8 and a fifth wave of 4, while the 16 empty tasks run in the other 4 slots, which are then idle: 5 waves of about 1.65 s is about 8.25 s, close to the 8.58 s measured. The 16 tasks that read nothing add only milliseconds.

What can make queries slow

Rows or totals into the Exchange?
From here on the lecture uses only the June 2012 trips, 15,096,468 of them (15.1 M), and steps run on 2 core nodes (8 slots):
trips       the June 2012 trips: 1 Parquet file, 8 row groups,

zones       the 265-row taxi zone table
broadcast   Spark automatically copies a table to every executor

## For each step on the June 2012 trips, what goes into an `Exchange` (shuffle)? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- count and average per payment type: `groupBy().agg()` :: partial totals
    > Each task totals its own rows first and sends one row per payment type it saw, a count and a sum, for the final stage to add up. The 8 reading tasks send 40 rows for the 15.1 M trips.
- number of trips per pickup day: `groupBy().count()` :: partial totals
    > Each task totals its own rows first and sends one row per pickup day it saw, a count (a sum of ones), for the final stage to add up: at most 30 rows per task, one for each day of June.
- each trip gets its payment type's average next to it: a window query :: every row
    > Every row goes into the `Exchange`, because no task can compute partial totals first: Spark puts the payment type's average next to every trip. All 15,096,468 trips, 86.5 MB, went into the `Exchange`.
- join the trips to another large table, over 10 MiB :: every row
    > Every row goes into the `Exchange`: neither table is small enough for Spark to copy, so both send their rows by the join key. With broadcast turned off, the trips joined to the zone table sent all 15.1 M trips, 88 MB.
- join the trips to the 265-row zone table: `F.broadcast(zones)` :: no shuffle `Exchange`
    > No trip rows move between Spark partitions: each task matches the rows in its own Spark partition against the copied 265-row table. The plan's `BroadcastExchange` copies the 265-row zone table to every executor, while a shuffle `Exchange` would repartition the trips by key.
- keep only the trips for the first week of June 2012 and calculate two new columns from values in each row :: no shuffle `Exchange`
    > No trip rows move between Spark partitions: each task filters its own rows and computes the two columns within its own Spark partition.
- :: one average per task
    > With one average per payment type from each task, the final stage could only average the averages, which is wrong when the tasks hold different numbers of trips (L5). A task sends a count and a sum instead, which the final stage adds up and divides.

Checks for a slow stage

Which change fixes a hot key, and which a spill?
A later query joins the June 2012 trips to the 5-row payment-type names table, a CSV file, with Spark’s automatic broadcast turned off. The query runs on 2 core nodes (8 slots) and takes 1.65 s. The Spark UI’s stage page shows these measurements for the stage after the Exchange (shuffle):
tasks             3; adaptive execution merged payment types 4 and 5
                  into the other two
records           7.8 million in one task, the trips paid by cash;
                  7.2 million in one, paid by card;
                  about 36,000 in the third, payment type 3
other slots       idle while the two large tasks run

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Cash and card are hot keys because millions of rows with each key go to one task. Which change shortens the query the most?

1. [x] Broadcast the names table
    > Copying the names table to every executor keeps the trips out of the `Exchange` and in their Spark partitions, so each task joins its own rows. With automatic broadcast off, `F.broadcast(names)` tells Spark to copy the names table. On the same cluster the query took 0.71 s with the broadcast and 1.65 s without; case P2.2 lists broadcast first, adaptive execution second and a salt third. The salted copy does not help the join, because its salt column was dropped before the write, so every cash trip still goes to one task.
1. [ ] Give each task more memory
    > Picking more memory assumes the two long tasks spilled. Adding memory does not move rows: all cash trips still go to one task, which still processes all 7.8 million of them.
1. [ ] Run the join on the salted copy of the trips (the June 2012 trips written as several files in each payment-type folder partition)
    > Several files per payment type let more tasks share the scan, but the salted copy has no salt column: the salt was dropped before the write. The join still sends every cash row to one task by payment type, however many shuffle partitions or nodes there are. To split a hot key in a join, a salt is added to both tables when the join runs (case P2.2).

Another query sorts the June 2012 trips by pickup time, on the same cluster but with each executor given 1 GiB of memory. A spill occurs when a task’s share of executor memory is too small, so the task writes intermediate data to the node’s disk. The stage after the Exchange shows these measurements:
shuffle partitions  8, set with spark.sql.shuffle.partitions
tasks             8
task duration     median 2.4 s, longest 2.6 s
records           about 1.9 million in every task
Spill (disk)      about 150 MB in every task
GC time           about 0.8 s in every task

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Every task spilled, and the tasks are of even size, so the cause is memory per task. Which change helps?

1. [ ] Fewer shuffle partitions, so fewer tasks compete for memory
    > Fewer shuffle partitions put more rows in each task. With 4 instead of 8, each task holds twice the rows and gets at most twice the memory, so each task still has too little memory, and 4 of the 8 slots are idle.
1. [ ] Write the input with more row groups
    > Row groups change the scan, not the stage after the `Exchange`. File sizes and slots set the number of scan tasks, and row groups decide how many scan tasks find rows. The number of shuffle partitions sets the rows per task after the `Exchange`.
1. [x] More shuffle partitions, so each task holds fewer rows
    > More shuffle partitions reduce the rows per task after the `Exchange`. On EMR, setting `spark.sql.shuffle.partitions` explicitly turns off adaptive execution's merging of shuffle partitions, so Spark keeps all 16. With 16 shuffle partitions, the stage runs 16 tasks of about 0.95 million rows, each needing half as much memory; giving each task more memory also works (Problem 4). More shuffle partitions help here because the tasks are of even size; rows with one key still go to one task, so more shuffle partitions do not split a hot key.

title: L6 review: how Spark runs a query, and why it might be slow
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Spark: shuffles and slow stages
Narrow transformation. A step each task does on its own partition, so no rows move between partitions: filter, select, withColumn.
Wide transformation. A step that needs rows from other partitions, such as groupBy, orderBy, a window or most joins. Spark adds a shuffle before it.
Shuffle (Exchange). Moving rows between partitions for the next stage: each task writes its rows to its node’s disk, and the next stage’s tasks read them, often from other nodes.
Window query. A step that computes a value over a group of rows and puts it on each row, such as each trip’s payment-type average next to the trip. Every row goes into an Exchange.
Hot key. One join, window or sort value with far more rows than the others. All its rows go to one task, which runs long after the rest of its stage; more nodes do not help.
Spill. Writing to the node’s disk when the rows a task sorts, groups or shuffles do not fit in its share of executor memory. The result is correct but slower.


Spark: how a job runs
Driver. The program that coordinates a Spark application: it runs your code, builds the query plan and sends tasks to the executors.
Executor. A Spark program running on an EMR core or task node. It runs tasks and keeps their data in its memory or on the node’s disk.
Partition. A chunk of rows that one task processes as one unit. When reading files it holds one or more splits, each a byte range of one file, planned from the file sizes and the number of slots.
Task. One stage’s work on one chunk of rows, run in one slot: by default, one executor core.
Slot. One executor core, as room to run one task on one Spark partition at a time. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks at once; our EMR nodes have one per vCPU.
Stage. A set of tasks Spark can run before rows have to move between partitions. Every task in it runs the same steps on a different partition.
Wave. The set of a stage’s tasks that run at the same time, one per slot. 36 reading tasks on 8 slots need 5 of them.
Transformation. A step such as filter or groupBy(...).count() that is only recorded in the plan. No task runs until an action asks for a result.
Action. On a Spark DataFrame, a call such as df.count(), df.collect() or df.write.parquet() that makes Spark run the plan built so far. Unlike pandas, where each step runs as soon as you call it.


EMR cluster
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node. The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node. An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node. An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing HDFS data.


Also used on this page
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Row group. A horizontal block inside one Parquet file, holding one column chunk per column. Its size is set when the file is written, and a file can hold one or many.
Folder partition. A dataset layout with one named location per value of a column, such as day=2012-06-14/ (on S3, a prefix). A filter on that column skips the other locations without opening them.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.

## For each workload, choose the engine that fits it best. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Analysts occasionally ask new questions about trip history data, without idle billing :: Athena
  > Athena bills per TB of Data scanned and charges nothing between queries, which suits best ad-hoc queries. S3 storage is billed either way.
- Nightly job rewrites yesterday's trips into a sorted Iceberg table. It runs for about 10 minutes :: Glue job
  > A Glue job bills DPU-hours for the run only, so a regular batch pays for its 10 minutes and nothing else.
- Dashboard executes the same 20 large-scan queries every few minutes, all day :: Trino on EMR
  > Calculate the crossover first: at this load the cluster, billed per node-hour, costs less than paying per query (the review page works the numbers).
- :: Lambda
  > With custom layers and the maximum memory setting you might be able to run some of these workloads in Lambda. However, it is not the best solution for any of them.

title: L12 review: DynamoDB as OLTP storage, distributed database problems and properties
text:
Which store fits each workload?
Operational and analytical stores side by side: DynamoDB, a relational database, S3 and the lakehouse.

---
shuffle_answers: true

## Match each workload to the store that fits it best. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- A game keeps each player's score as one small record, updated by player id tens of thousands of times a second at peak. Nothing joins it to other data :: DynamoDB
  > Small items, always found by one key, at a rate that changes with the game: what DynamoDB is built for.
- A shopping site reads and writes each visitor's cart by cart id on every page view, with ten times the traffic on sale days. No query joins carts :: DynamoDB
  > One key per request and traffic that jumps: DynamoDB scales on demand and answers in milliseconds.
- An order system runs one query that joins customers, orders and products :: Relational database (RDS)
  > Joins across tables are what a relational database does. DynamoDB has no joins.
- A video site stores each uploaded video, files of several gigabytes :: S3
  > A DynamoDB item is at most 400 KB. Large files go to S3, as objects.
- Analysts ask a new SQL question every week over 5 TB of order history from three years :: Lakehouse (Athena on Iceberg)
  > Ad hoc questions that scan a lot of history: columns in Parquet, billed by Data scanned.
- A nightly report adds up about 3 TB of sales records by product :: Lakehouse (Athena on Iceberg)
  > A scan of terabytes on DynamoDB would read every item, for hours and dollars. The lakehouse reads only the columns the report needs.

text:
Which reads need a strong read?
Reads in the trip app: when a read may be a moment old, and when it must return the latest write.

---
shuffle_answers: true

## For each read in the trip app, choose the least expensive option that meets its need. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The driver app reads trip t-0042 back right after its own accept succeeded, to show the assigned driver :: Strongly consistent read
  > Read-after-write: an eventual read might come from a replica without the accept and show the trip still "requested".
- The driver app shows whether the passenger has cancelled, right after the passenger phoned the driver to say so :: Strongly consistent read
  > Another user's write the driver already knows about: an eventual read could still show the trip as active.
- The passenger app refreshes the driver's position on the map every two seconds, where an old position is acceptable :: Eventually consistent read
  > An old position is acceptable here, later refreshes replace it, and eventual reads cost half.
- The passenger app shows the fare right after the passenger's promo-code update succeeded :: Strongly consistent read
  > Read-after-write: the passenger just wrote, and an old fare on screen would look like the promo failed.
- A list of the passenger's past trips, where a trip that just finished may appear on the next refresh :: Eventually consistent read
  > An old list is acceptable on this screen, and eventual reads cost half.
- :: Federated query from Athena
  > A query taking seconds through a connector serves reports, not a screen that must open in milliseconds.

title: L12 review: DynamoDB as OLTP storage, distributed database problems and properties
text:
Which problem is each situation?
A food-delivery app keeps live orders in DynamoDB and order history in a lakehouse.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A food-delivery app keeps orders in a database copied across two Regions and order history in a lakehouse. Match each situation to the problem it shows. Not all options will be used.

- A customer's address change succeeds, and an eventually consistent read on the confirmation screen right after shows the old address :: Replication lag
  > The read came from a replica that did not have the write yet. No link failed. A strongly consistent read would have shown the new address.
- Two couriers both read the order as "ready" and mark it "picked up", and the order ends up with the second courier's name :: Lost update
  > Both couriers read the order before either wrote. The second write replaced the first. A conditional write would have refused one.
- A nightly load into the lakehouse runs twice after a timeout, and yesterday's orders appear twice :: Non-idempotent load
  > Running the load again adds the same orders again. An idempotent load (a `MERGE` keyed by order id over deduplicated input) leaves one copy of each.
- The link between two Regions fails, and the app in one Region returns errors for order updates until the link is back :: Netsplit
  > The cut-off Region refuses writes, so the two Regions never disagree. That is the consistency choice in a netsplit (CAP). DynamoDB, in this case, would by default keep taking writes in both Regions and settle conflicting writes later: the last writer wins.
- :: Hot partition
  > One partition key taking most of the traffic overloads one storage partition. None of these situations is about load on one key.
- :: Write lost in failover
  > A write is lost in failover when the leader fails before any follower has it. In none of these situations does a leader fail.
