text:
Learning from practice
I recommend to go through Block 3’s Tutorials 1 and 2 before starting this section.

Which statement runs each operation?

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## An online shop keeps its orders in an Iceberg table. Match each operation to the Athena statement that runs it. Not all options will be used.

- Remove the orders of closed accounts :: `DELETE FROM orders WHERE …`
  > Athena's `DELETE` writes delete files that mark the removed rows. The data files stay as they were. See Tutorial 2, [Step 3](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-3-delete-some-rows).
- Merge small files, and files with deleted rows, into fewer larger files :: `OPTIMIZE orders REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK`
  > Bin-packing, merging files up to a target size, is the only way Athena compacts a table. See Tutorial 2, [Step 4](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-4-compact-the-table).
- Drop snapshots older than a set age, and delete the files that no remaining snapshot uses :: `VACUUM orders`
  > One statement does both. The table property `vacuum_max_snapshot_age_seconds` sets how old a snapshot must be. See Tutorial 2, [Step 5](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-5-remove-the-old-files-for-good).
- Add a column for the delivery method :: `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMNS (delivery string)`
  > Only the table's metadata changes. No data file is rewritten. See Tutorial 1, [Step 5](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t1-athena-rides#step-5-add-a-column).
- :: `COMPACT TABLE orders`
  > Athena has no `COMPACT` statement. Compaction is `OPTIMIZE`.
- :: `EXPIRE SNAPSHOTS orders`
  > Athena has no such statement. `VACUUM` expires snapshots.

## The same shop runs maintenance from a Glue job in Spark. Iceberg's maintenance procedures run with `CALL`, through the Iceberg catalog, which this job names `glue_catalog`. Match each operation to the Spark statement that runs it. Not all options will be used.

- Remove the orders of closed accounts :: `DELETE FROM orders WHERE …`
  > `DELETE` is also Athena's statement. By default Spark rewrites the data files that held the rows (copy-on-write), unless the table property `write.delete.mode` is `merge-on-read`, which writes delete files as Athena does.
- Merge small files, and files with deleted rows, into fewer larger files :: `CALL glue_catalog.system.rewrite_data_files(…)`
  > Iceberg's compaction procedure. Athena's `OPTIMIZE` takes none of these settings, and this procedure takes a strategy, a sort order and a target file size.
- Drop snapshots older than a set age, and delete the files that no remaining snapshot uses :: `CALL glue_catalog.system.expire_snapshots(…)`
  > It drops the snapshots and deletes the files that only those snapshots used.
- Delete files in the table's folder that no snapshot ever listed, such as files left by a failed write :: `CALL glue_catalog.system.remove_orphan_files(…)`
  > These are orphan files. The procedure can list them first with `dry_run => true`. Athena's `VACUUM` deletes them directly.
- :: `CALL glue_catalog.system.optimize(…)`
  > Iceberg has no `optimize` procedure. `OPTIMIZE` is Athena's name for compaction, and Spark with Iceberg uses `rewrite_data_files`.
- :: `CALL glue_catalog.system.vacuum(…)`
  > Iceberg has no `vacuum` procedure. `VACUUM` is Athena's name, and in Spark the same work is two calls, `expire_snapshots` and `remove_orphan_files`.



What does each operation change?
The shop’s orders table has one folder per order day. Each hour a job appends a few small files, and last week the shop deleted, in Athena, the orders of customers who closed their accounts.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each goal, choose the operation that achieves it. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Queries no longer read the delete files from last week's deletions :: Compaction
  > Compaction rewrites each data file without its deleted rows, so later queries have no delete files to read. In Athena: `OPTIMIZE`. In Spark: `rewrite_data_files`, then `rewrite_position_delete_files` to clear delete files that still point at rewritten data files. See Tutorial 2, [Step 4](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-4-compact-the-table).
- Each day's many small files become a few large files :: Compaction
  > Compaction merges small files up to a target size. In Athena: `OPTIMIZE`. In Spark: `rewrite_data_files`, which can also sort the rows. See Tutorial 2, [Step 4](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-4-compact-the-table).
- Files in S3 take less space than before last week's deletions :: Snapshot expiry
  > The old files stay in S3 while an older snapshot still lists them. Snapshot expiry drops those snapshots and deletes the files only they used. In Athena: `VACUUM`. In Spark: `expire_snapshots`. See Tutorial 2, [Step 5](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-5-remove-the-old-files-for-good).
- Time-travel queries can no longer return the deleted orders :: Snapshot expiry
  > Until the old snapshots are expired, a time-travel query can still read the files that hold those orders. In Athena: `VACUUM`. In Spark: `expire_snapshots`. See Tutorial 1, [Step 3](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t1-athena-rides#step-3-change-your-copy-then-look-back) and Tutorial 2, [Step 5](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-5-remove-the-old-files-for-good).
- :: Deleting rows
  > Deleting rows, with `DELETE` in Athena and Spark, adds new files and keeps the old ones in S3, so on its own it meets none of these goals. See Tutorial 2, [Step 3](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-3-delete-some-rows).

## The shop runs one `DELETE` on the orders table in Athena. Which statements are true right after it? Select all that apply.

- [x] No data file was rewritten
    > Athena writes delete files that mark the rows. It does not rewrite the data files. See Tutorial 2, [Step 3](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-3-delete-some-rows).
- [x] More files in the table than before
    > Each `DELETE` statement adds delete files. Compaction later folds them into rewritten data files.
- [x] Time travel to before the `DELETE` shows the deleted rows
    > The earlier snapshot lists the same data files and none of the new delete files. See Tutorial 1, [Step 3](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t1-athena-rides#step-3-change-your-copy-then-look-back).
- [ ] Less storage in S3 than before
    > Nothing is removed from S3. The delete files add a little storage.
- [ ] Queries read fewer files than before
    > Queries now read the delete files as well as the data files, until compaction.

## You run compaction (`OPTIMIZE`) and then list the table's folder in S3. It holds more data than before. Why?

1. [x] Earlier snapshots still list the old data and delete files
    > Compaction writes new files and commits a new snapshot. The old files still belong to earlier snapshots until snapshot expiry (`VACUUM`) drops them. In Spark: `expire_snapshots`. See Tutorial 2, [Step 4](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-4-compact-the-table) and Tutorial 2, [Step 5](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-5-remove-the-old-files-for-good).
1. [ ] Compaction keeps the delete files, which now apply to the new files
    > The new files are written without the deleted rows, so the new snapshot lists no delete files. The old delete files stay only for the earlier snapshots.
1. [ ] Compaction keeps a backup copy of the table for safety
    > No backup is made. Compaction writes only the new, merged files.



Athena or Spark?

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each maintenance need on an Iceberg table, choose where you can do it. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Compact only one day's folder, not the whole table :: Athena or Spark
  > Athena's `OPTIMIZE … WHERE` on the day column, or Spark's `rewrite_data_files` with a `where` filter.
- Sort the rows inside each file by order time during compaction :: Spark only
  > Athena's `OPTIMIZE` only merges files and keeps the rows in the order they were written. Spark's `rewrite_data_files` takes `strategy => 'sort'`.
- Choose the target size of the files that compaction writes :: Spark only
  > Athena picks the target size itself, and none of its table properties sets it. Spark's `rewrite_data_files` takes `target-file-size-bytes`.
- Compact only the files holding one store's orders, when the table has one folder per day, not per store :: Spark only
  > Athena's `WHERE` in `OPTIMIZE` accepts only the columns the folders are named by. Spark's `where` filter can name other columns.
- Expire snapshots older than a set age :: Athena or Spark
  > Athena's `VACUUM` uses the table property `vacuum_max_snapshot_age_seconds`. Spark's `expire_snapshots` takes `older_than` in each call.
- List orphan files, which no snapshot ever listed, before deleting them :: Spark only
  > Spark's `remove_orphan_files` with `dry_run => true`. Athena's `VACUUM` deletes them directly.
- Run maintenance as queries in the query editor, without starting a job or a notebook session :: Athena only
  > Athena runs `OPTIMIZE` and `VACUUM` as queries. Spark needs a Glue job or a notebook session. See Tutorial 2, [Step 4](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-4-compact-the-table).
- Pay for compaction by scanned data amount instead of worker time :: Athena only
  > Athena bills `OPTIMIZE` by the data scanned during the rewrite. A Glue job or session bills its DPUs for the time it runs.
- :: Neither
  > Each need here can be met in Athena, Spark or both.



How a job writes and reloads a table

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## A Glue job reads a week of orders and calls `repartition(8)`, which spreads the rows evenly over 8 Spark partitions without looking at their day. So each Spark partition holds orders from all seven days. The job writes them to a table with one folder per day, with `write.distribution-mode = none`, so Spark does not regroup the rows by day before writing. How many files does each day's folder get?

1. [x] 8, one from each task
    > Each task writes one file into every day folder it has rows for, and here every task has rows for every day. See Tutorial 2, [Step 1](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-1-start-the-job-then-read-it-while-it-runs) and Tutorial 2, [Step 2](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-2-check-what-the-job-built).
1. [ ] One
    > One file per day needs the rows regrouped by day before writing, which `write.distribution-mode = hash` does.
1. [ ] 56, eight for each of the seven days
    > 56 is the number of files for the whole week, across all seven folders.

## A Glue job appends one day of orders to the table on each run. A run finishes successfully, and then someone presses **Run** in the console again. What does the table hold?

1. [x] Every order of that day twice
    > An append doesn't check what is already loaded. To make the load safe to repeat, delete that day before writing it, as you did to repair the double load in Tutorial 1. A `MERGE` on a key also works. See Tutorial 1, [Step 4](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t1-athena-rides#step-4-load-the-same-day-twice-then-repair) and Tutorial 2, [Step 1](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/b3-t2-glue-rides#step-1-start-the-job-then-read-it-while-it-runs).
1. [ ] Every order of that day once, because Iceberg skips duplicate rows
    > Iceberg has no unique-key check on append.
1. [ ] Every order of that day once, because Glue stops a duplicate job run by default
    > By default Glue allows one run of a job at a time, so it refuses a second start only while the first run is still going. After the first run succeeds, the second run starts and appends the day again.

title: L12 review: DynamoDB as OLTP storage, distributed database problems and properties
text:
Terms used on this page
System of record. The store with the authoritative copy; other copies are derived from it.
Operational system (OLTP), analytical system (OLAP), point query. Many small reads and writes by key, in milliseconds; scans and aggregates over many records; one record fetched by its key.
Row-oriented, column-oriented. One record’s values stored together; one column’s values stored together.
Item, partition key, sort key. DynamoDB’s record; the key part that picks its storage partition; the optional part that orders items sharing a partition key.
GetItem, Query, Scan. One item by key; the items of one partition key; every item.
Read request unit / write request unit. One strong read (or two eventual) of up to 4 KB; one write of up to 1 KB.
Export, federated query, derived copy. A copy of the store’s items written to S3 (all, or those changed in a time window); a query that reads the store through a connector; a result computed elsewhere and written back.
Partial failure, timeout, netsplit. Some parts fail; giving up waiting; nodes that cannot reach each other.
Replication, sharding. The same data on several nodes; a different slice on each node.
Replica, leader, follower. A copy on another node; in single-leader replication, the one that takes writes; the ones that copy from it.
Region, Availability Zone (AZ). A geographic area; one or more isolated data centres (buildings of nodes) in a Region, with their own power and network.
Synchronous, asynchronous, majority (quorum). “done” after the required followers have it; after the leader’s own commit; after more than half have it.
Replication lag, eventual consistency, read-after-write. A follower behind the leader; agreement if writes stop, no deadline; your reads show your writes.
Linearizability. Behaves as one copy, in real-time order; “strong consistency” is a vague name for it.
Eventually / strongly consistent read. Any replica, may be old, 0.5 units per 4 KB; the leader, the latest value including every write finished before the read, 1 unit per 4 KB.
CAP, PACELC. During a netsplit, linearizable or a non-error answer from every working node; else, latency or consistency.
Lost update, compare-and-set, conditional write, optimistic concurrency. The second write replaces the first; write only if unchanged; DynamoDB’s form; check at the end, retry if changed.
Transaction, ACID, BASE. A group that succeeds or fails whole; atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability; mostly “not ACID”.
Serializability. The outcome of concurrent transactions equals running them one at a time.
Timeliness, integrity, idempotent. Shows the latest; nothing lost or duplicated; twice has the effect of once.

section: How Spark divides and coordinates the work
text:
How Spark divides and coordinates the work

What does Spark run again when a core node is lost? *
A Spark query over a year of lift-gate scans in S3 counts the scans per gate, so its scan stage is followed by an Exchange (shuffle). The query runs on an EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge, with the driver on core node 1. Each core node has an executor, a process that runs 4 tasks at a time (8 slots in total). The query’s scan stage has 36 tasks, each reading one Spark partition of the input: one or more byte ranges of the files in S3. The task counts just before the failure were:
scan stage, 36 tasks      finished   running   not started
core node 1                  10         4
core node 2                  10         4
total                        20         8           8
Then core node 2 fails, and its executor and its disk are lost.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After the core node 2 failure, besides the 8 tasks that have not started, how many scan tasks does Spark run again?

1. [x] 14
    > When core node 2 was lost, its 4 running tasks stopped and the output of its 10 finished tasks was also lost. Spark reruns the 14 tasks of core node 2, each rereading its Spark partition from S3; the output of core node 1's finished tasks stays available.
1. [ ] 4
    > Choosing 4 treats a finished task's output as safe. A finished scan task's output is stored on its node for the next stage; if the node is lost, the output is also lost, so Spark reruns the task.
1. [ ] 36
    > Choosing 36 reruns every task, as when a query in one process on one instance fails and is rerun from the start. Spark can reread the input's Spark partitions from S3, so it reruns only the tasks whose work was lost.
1. [ ] 28
    > Core node 1 still has its executor and its disk, so the output of its 10 finished tasks remains and its 4 running tasks continue. Only core node 2's work is lost.

Slide: 10 (also 8)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Amazon EMR

How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?
An EMR cluster has three kinds of nodes, all m7g.xlarge with 4 vCPUs each, at $0.2227 an hour per node (on demand in ca-central-1, EC2 plus EMR’s fee):
primary   1 node
core      4 nodes
task      3 nodes
A node hosts at most one executor, which gets 4 cores, one per vCPU of the node, and so runs 4 tasks at a time (4 slots).

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## How many tasks can the cluster run at once (how many slots does it have)?

1. [x] 28
    > The 4 core nodes and 3 task nodes host executors, so 7 × 4 = 28 tasks run at once. The primary node manages the cluster and hosts no executor. You pay for 8 nodes, about \$1.78 an hour at \$0.2227 each, and 7 of them run tasks.
1. [ ] 32
    > Choosing 32 counts the primary node as a node that runs tasks. The primary node manages the cluster and hosts no executor.
1. [ ] 56
    > Choosing 56 gives each node 8 slots, two per vCPU. On our m7g nodes one vCPU is one physical processor core, and an executor gets one slot per vCPU: 4 per node.
1. [ ] 12
    > Choosing 12 assumes that only task nodes host executors. Core nodes also host executors and store blocks for the Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS), while task nodes host executors without storing HDFS data.

Slide: 18, 19 (also 11, 16)

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Spark, PySpark and Spark SQL

What runs where: the plan, an action, or pandas on the driver
A notebook on an EMR cluster works with a bike-share company’s rides, stored as Parquet files on S3. Earlier cells left two DataFrames in the notebook:
per_city   Spark DataFrame    ride counts per city, built earlier
                              from the rides files
stations   pandas DataFrame   docks per station, with each station's city
F is pyspark.sql.functions.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each line, what happens when its cell runs? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `rides = spark.read.parquet("s3://…/bikeshare/rides/")` :: Spark builds the plan on the driver; no ride rows are read
    > The driver lists the files and puts the read into the plan; a one-task job reads one file's footer to learn the columns, and no ride rows are read until an action needs them.
- `per_city.explain()` :: Spark builds the plan on the driver; no ride rows are read
    > `.explain()` prints the plan recorded so far on the driver and reads no ride rows, so no task starts. Spark scans the rows only when an action needs them.
- `victoria = per_city.filter(F.col("city") == "Victoria")` :: Spark builds the plan on the driver; no ride rows are read
    > `filter` is a transformation: Spark adds the step to the plan on the driver and reads no rows, and no task starts until an action needs the rows.
- `top = per_city.toPandas()` :: Spark sends tasks that read the ride rows; they run now
    > `toPandas()` is an action: it needs the rows of `per_city`, so the driver creates tasks from the plan and the executors read and count the rides now.
- `rows = per_city.collect()` :: Spark sends tasks that read the ride rows; they run now
    > `.collect()` is an action: it needs the rows of `per_city`, so the driver creates tasks from the plan and the executors read and count the rides now.
- `stations.groupby("city")["docks"].sum()` :: pandas computes on the driver; no task runs
    > `stations` is a pandas DataFrame, and pandas has no Spark plan: the sum is computed in the driver's Python process, and no executor gets a task.
- `top.to_csv("per_city.csv")`, after `top = per_city.toPandas()` has already run :: pandas computes on the driver; no task runs
    > `top` holds the rows that `toPandas()` already brought to the driver, so `top` is a pandas DataFrame with no Spark plan. The file is written from the driver's Python process, and no executor gets a task.
- :: pandas computes on the executors, split across them
    > A cluster does not split a pandas operation across executors. pandas runs in the driver's Python process and creates no Spark task.

A delivery company keeps its fees in one 1 GB Parquet file on S3. You have a PySpark notebook in JupyterHub open in your laptop’s browser, as in the lecture: Livy sends the notebook’s cells to the Spark driver. The notebook runs on an EMR cluster of 1 primary and 2 core nodes, all m7g.xlarge with 4 vCPUs and 16 GiB of memory each. A cell reads the file with pandas:
fees = pd.read_parquet("s3://…/delivery/fees.parquet")

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Where are the rows of `fees` held, and what is the most memory the cell can use?

1. [x] In the driver's Python process, within one node's 16 GiB
    > Every cell of a PySpark notebook runs in the Spark driver. pandas works in the driver's Python process on one node, so the other nodes' memory does not help, and the process may be allocated less than the node's 16 GiB.
1. [ ] Across both core nodes' executors, within 32 GiB in total
    > Executors get work from Spark only through an action or the short job that reads a file's footer at `spark.read`. A pandas call is not Spark: no task is created, so the rows never leave the driver.
1. [ ] On your laptop, where the notebook is open, within its memory
    > Choosing the laptop assumes local Jupyter, where Python runs on your laptop. On EMR the browser only sends cells and shows output: JupyterHub is on the primary node, and the cells run in the driver on a core node, so the rows of `fees` stay on the cluster.

Slide: 22, 24, 25 (also 16, 21)


What goes into the Exchange (shuffle)?
A ferry company keeps its 2025 ticket sales as one Parquet file on S3. Each row is one ticket:



sale_date
route
fare




2025-03-02
Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay
$8


2025-03-02
Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay

A PySpark query computes the average fare per route for March 2025; sales is the Spark DataFrame read from the file and F is pyspark.sql.functions:
march = sales.filter(F.col("sale_date").between("2025-03-01", "2025-03-31"))
by_route = march.groupBy("route").agg(F.avg("fare").alias("avg_fare"))
Each scan task reads one Spark partition of the file: one or more byte ranges of the file. Tickets are stored in the order they were sold, so a route’s tickets are spread over several tasks. The Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay route sold 4 tickets in March, for $60 in all, so its average fare is $15. Two tasks read the 4 tickets:




tickets
fares
sum
average




task 1
3
$8, $10, $12
$30

1

$30




---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## What should each task send into the `Exchange` (shuffle) so that the final stage computes \$15 from the least data?

1. [x] Count and sum of fares for the route
    > Task 1 sends 3 and \$30, task 2 sends 1 and \$30; the final stage adds them and divides: \$60 / 4 = \$15. Each task sends two numbers per route, however many tickets it reads. Partial totals are enough for a group-by sum, count or average; a window query or a join that regroups both tables by key sends every row into the `Exchange`, so one task receives all rows of each key.
1. [ ] Average of the task's fares for the route
    > The final stage would receive two averages, \$10 from task 1 and \$30 from task 2, and could only average them: (\$10 + \$30) / 2 = \$20, not \$15. The final stage cannot weight task 1's average by its 3 tickets because the count is not sent. An average of averages is wrong whenever the groups differ in size.
1. [ ] Every ticket row the task reads for the route
    > Sending every row into the `Exchange` also gives \$15, but sends more data. Partial totals give the same answer with two numbers per route from each task.

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Storage on the cluster

Where is each kind of data kept?
A team keeps Vancouver’s Van311 non-emergency service requests for 2025 as Parquet files on S3, and a notebook on an EMR cluster works with them:
cluster    1 primary + 2 core nodes
notebook   builds `late`, the requests that took more than 45 days to close
end        the cluster is terminated when the notebook's work ends

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Where is each kind of data kept? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- rows a task cannot fit in memory while it works :: the node's disk
    > Working data on a node's own disk is deleted when the cluster ends. A task that cannot fit its rows in memory spills them there and reads them back later.
- Spark's cache of a DataFrame once executor memory is full :: the node's disk
    > Working data on a node's own disk is deleted when the cluster ends. By default, Spark stores the cache in executor memory first and then on the node's disk once memory is full.
- the rows `.collect()` returns :: driver memory
    > The result is stored in the driver's process: the executors run the plan, and `.collect()` sends every row of the result to the driver.
- the number `late.count()` returns to the notebook :: driver memory
    > The result is stored in the driver's process: the executors run the plan and count the rows, and the driver receives the total as one Python number.
- the 2025 request files the notebook reads :: S3
    > The input was on S3 before the cluster started, and every executor reads its Spark partitions from there; S3 keeps the files after the cluster ends.
- the table of `late` requests that next week's report reads :: S3
    > The nodes' disks and HDFS are deleted with the cluster, so a result that next week's report reads is written to S3, which keeps it until someone deletes it.
- :: the cluster's HDFS
    > HDFS pools the core nodes' disks into one shared file system. A Spark job writes to HDFS only on purpose, such as a result the job rereads while the cluster runs, and HDFS is deleted with the cluster. Spills and Spark's cache go to the node's disk outside HDFS, and the table of late requests goes to S3 because next week's report reads it after the cluster is terminated. None of the listed data is stored in HDFS.

title: L5 review: Spark on a cluster
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise the terms in quiz mode, or try the match game.

Spark: how a job runs
Driver. The program that coordinates a Spark application: it runs your code, builds the query plan and sends tasks to the executors.
Executor. A Spark program running on an EMR core or task node. It runs tasks and keeps their data in its memory or on the node’s disk.
Partition. A chunk of rows that one task processes as one unit. When reading files it holds one or more splits, each a byte range of one file, planned from the file sizes and the number of slots.
Task. One stage’s work on one chunk of rows, run in one slot: by default, one executor core.
Slot. One executor core, as room to run one task on one Spark partition at a time. An executor with 4 cores runs 4 tasks at once; our EMR nodes have one per vCPU.
Stage. A set of tasks Spark can run before rows have to move between partitions. Every task in it runs the same steps on a different partition.
Wave. The set of a stage’s tasks that run at the same time, one per slot. 36 reading tasks on 8 slots need 5 of them.
Transformation. A step such as filter or groupBy(...).count() that is only recorded in the plan. No task runs until an action asks for a result.
Action. On a Spark DataFrame, a call such as df.count(), df.collect() or df.write.parquet() that makes Spark run the plan built so far. Unlike pandas, where each step runs as soon as you call it.


Spark: shuffles and slow stages
Narrow transformation. A step each task does on its own partition, so no rows move between partitions: filter, select, withColumn.
Wide transformation. A step that needs rows from other partitions, such as groupBy, orderBy, a window or most joins. Spark adds a shuffle before it.
Shuffle (Exchange). Moving rows between partitions for the next stage: each task writes its rows to its node’s disk, and the next stage’s tasks read them, often from other nodes.
Window query. A step that computes a value over a group of rows and puts it on each row, such as each trip’s payment-type average next to the trip. Every row goes into an Exchange.
Hot key. One join, window or sort value with far more rows than the others. All its rows go to one task, which runs long after the rest of its stage; more nodes do not help.
Spill. Writing to the node’s disk when the rows a task sorts, groups or shuffles do not fit in its share of executor memory. The result is correct but slower.


EMR cluster
Amazon EMR. AWS’s managed service that launches a cluster of EC2 instances with Spark installed. You pay for the nodes from launch until you terminate the cluster.
Primary node. The one EMR instance that runs the cluster manager and the HDFS name service. It runs no executors.
Core node. An EMR instance that runs executors and stores HDFS data. A role an instance plays in the cluster, not a Spark slot.
Task node. An optional EMR instance that runs executors and stores no HDFS data, so it can be removed or bought as spot capacity without losing HDFS data.
HDFS. A file system that splits files into blocks across a cluster’s core nodes’ disks. Its data is lost when the cluster terminates, so our inputs and outputs stay on S3.


Also used on this page
Parquet. A columnar file format. Rows are grouped into blocks that each store every column separately, and metadata at the end of the file says where each part is.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.

title: L11 review: assembling the lakehouse in Athena and Glue
text: If you need to look up a term, the relevant vocabulary is below.

title: L11 review: assembling the lakehouse in Athena and Glue
text:
Recap of L10

Which layer does each tool or format belong to?
In a lakehouse, your files stay in your own storage, and you pick a separate tool or format for each part that a cloud warehouse supplies as one service. Each tool or format below belongs to one of those parts.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Put each tool or format on its layer of a lakehouse. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Parquet :: Storage format
  > Parquet encodes the rows of one data file, column by column, with a footer. The table format (Iceberg) is the metadata above many such files.
- Spark :: Query engine
  > Spark SQL plans the query and runs the plan. On EMR, a cluster manager (YARN) starts Spark's executors on the cluster's nodes; YARN runs under the engine and is not a layer of the lakehouse.
- S3 :: Object storage
  > S3 stores data files and metadata files as objects; the table's metadata records which files form the table.
- Iceberg :: Table format
  > Iceberg's metadata files list the data files in the table's current snapshot, with the schema and the snapshots. Parquet encodes the rows.
- Trino :: Query engine
  > Trino plans the SQL query and runs the plan on its workers. A connector gives Trino access to one source, such as a data lake or a database, so it is part of the engine, not a layer of the lakehouse.
- Glue Data Catalog :: Catalog
  > The Glue Data Catalog lists tables and points each Iceberg table to its current metadata file.
- :: Cluster manager
  > A cluster manager (YARN on EMR, L5) starts Spark's executors on the nodes. It runs under the engine and is not one of the lakehouse's parts.
- :: Connector
  > In Trino a connector is how the engine reads one source, for example the Glue Data Catalog (L10). It belongs to the engine, not to a layer of its own.



Data lake, lakehouse, or both?
An online shop’s orders, kept two ways. In the data lake, the table is a folder of Parquet files in S3, one subfolder per day. In the lakehouse, the table is an Iceberg table in the Glue Data Catalog over those Parquet files, partitioned by the day of order_time. Athena reads both tables and changes the Iceberg table.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Does each statement describe the data lake, the lakehouse, or both? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- The rows are stored as Parquet objects in an S3 bucket :: Both
  > Both keep Parquet files in S3. The difference is the table format and the catalog above them.
- A query skips day folders only if its filter uses the folder partition column :: Data lake
  > In a data lake the engine can skip day folders only when the filter uses the folder partition column (P2). An Iceberg table's partition value is derived from the order time (Iceberg partitioning), so a filter on the order time skips other days.
- A delete adds a small file that lists the removed rows, and the data file is not changed :: Lakehouse
  > Iceberg calls it a delete file, and Athena's `DELETE` on an Iceberg table writes one (P4). Readers skip the rows it lists, and the data file itself is not changed. A folder of Parquet files has no delete files: changing a row means writing a new copy of its file.
- A query can read the table as it was last Friday, while that snapshot is still retained :: Lakehouse
  > Iceberg keeps each snapshot until it is expired, and time travel reads an earlier one (P5). A folder has no snapshots, so nothing records which files formed the table last Friday.
- A data file is not edited after it is written :: Both
  > In both, a Parquet file is never edited once written. The lakehouse adds delete files or new data files instead (P4).
- A reader lists the folder and reads whatever files are there now :: Data lake
  > A folder has no table commit that makes all files of one write visible together, so a reader can see part of a write (P1). An Iceberg reader finds the data files through the current snapshot's manifests instead of listing the folder.
- :: Neither
  > Every statement here describes the data lake, the lakehouse, or both of them.

title: L11 review: assembling the lakehouse in Athena and Glue
text:
Open-source parts and AWS services

Which AWS service runs or keeps each part?
An online shop keeps its orders as an Iceberg table of Parquet files in S3, registered in the Glue Data Catalog, and reads and changes it with different AWS services.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Each row is open-source software or an open file format from L10's layers, used on AWS. Match each row to the AWS service that runs it or keeps it for you. Not all options will be used.

- Trino plans and runs your SQL on the orders table; you start no cluster and pay for the query's Data scanned :: Athena
  > Athena's engine (version 3) is built on Trino, which is open source. AWS adds everything around the engine: no cluster to start, the workgroup and its Data scanned limit, and the bill per TB of Data scanned.
- Spark runs your PySpark script; you choose a worker type and a number of workers and pay per DPU-hour :: AWS Glue job
  > An AWS Glue job runs Apache Spark. PySpark code that uses only Spark APIs is portable to Spark on EMR or a laptop; Glue-specific setup and APIs such as `GlueContext` and `job.commit` must be removed or replaced.
- Spark runs a PySpark script on a cluster whose node types you choose; each node is billed per second while the cluster is up :: EMR
  > EMR starts EC2 instances and installs open-source software on them: Spark (L5), and also Trino or Hive if you ask. You choose the nodes, and they are billed while up, busy or idle.
- An Iceberg table needs one place that records which metadata file is current; Athena, Glue jobs and EMR all look it up there :: Glue Data Catalog
  > Iceberg's metadata files are files in your bucket; the pointer to the current one lives in a catalog, and on AWS that catalog is the Glue Data Catalog. On another cloud the Iceberg files come along and the catalog is replaced.
- The Parquet data files and Iceberg's metadata files of the orders table are stored as objects :: S3
  > Parquet and Iceberg are open formats, so any engine that reads them can read these files. S3 keeps them and bills per GB-month.
- :: Lambda
  > Lambda runs a function for each event; it runs none of these engines or tables.
- :: Redshift
  > Redshift is AWS's data warehouse, where one vendor provides every layer (L10); it is not the service behind any row here.

title: L11 review: assembling the lakehouse in Athena and Glue
text:
Which fix handles which situation

Which lakehouse feature handles each situation in an online shop’s orders table?
An online shop keeps its orders in an Iceberg table in the Glue Data Catalog, over Parquet files in S3. Each order has an order_time, and the table is partitioned by the day of order_time. A load adds new orders every hour, and corrections change rows. Athena reads and changes the table.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Match each situation to the lakehouse feature that handles it. Not all options will be used.

- An auditor asks what yesterday's total sales were before this morning's correction, while that snapshot is still retained :: Time travel
  > Each data change creates a snapshot that is kept until it is expired, and a query can read the snapshot that was current before the correction (P5).
- After weeks of hourly loads the table holds thousands of small files, and every query starts slowly :: Compaction
  > Compaction rewrites many small data files into fewer larger ones (P3). The manifests already save the folder listing; the small files are what remains to fix.
- A dashboard query runs while a load is adding new orders; it must show all of that load or none of it :: Table commit
  > The load becomes visible in one step, when the catalog entry switches to the new metadata file (P1).
- Test orders must disappear from the table, and the data files that hold them must not be changed :: Delete files
  > A delete file is a small file that lists which rows of a data file are deleted; readers skip those rows, and the data file itself is not changed. Athena's `DELETE` writes one (P4, no change or delete in place). The `DELETE` is also a commit, but the commit alone does not say how rows are removed.
- A query filters on `order_time` for one afternoon and opens only that day's data files, without naming any folder :: Iceberg partitioning
  > The table is partitioned by the day of `order_time`, a value Iceberg derives from the column (hidden partitioning), so a filter on the column itself skips other days' files (P2).
- :: `_SUCCESS` file
  > Spark writes it at the end of a job, but readers of a folder do not check it by default, so it does not make a write all-or-nothing.
- :: Folder partition column
  > The data lake's workaround for P2: it skips day folders only when the query's filter uses the folder partition column.

title: L11 review: assembling the lakehouse in Athena and Glue
text:
Which levels skip data

Which levels skip data for each query?
An online shop’s orders table is an Iceberg table of Parquet files, partitioned by the day of order_time. Each day’s rows are written sorted by order_time, in row groups that each cover a short stretch of the day. Each row has order_time, customer_id, category, total and a dozen other columns. Athena runs each query below.

---
shuffle_answers: false
---

## Query: number of orders in each hour of last Monday. Which levels skip data? Select all that apply.

- [x] Files (manifests)
    > The filter covers last Monday, so the manifests keep that day's files and skip every other day's.
- [ ] Row groups (footer minimum and maximum)
    > The filter covers the whole day, so every row group of Monday's files holds rows the query needs.
- [x] Columns (projection)
    > The query needs only `order_time`, for the filter and for the hour; Athena does not read the other columns.
- [ ] None: no level skips data
    > The manifests keep last Monday's files, and the query reads one column: files and columns both skip.

## Query: the `total` values for last Monday's orders whose `total` is above \$500. Every row group in Monday's files contains at least one such order. Which levels skip data? Select all that apply.

- [x] Files (manifests)

text:
Choosing an engine for a regular workload
Five steps, from naming the inputs to your own cost comparison (a crossover). Steps 1 and 2 are quizzes; step 3 is a worked example to read; in step 4 you finish one; step 5 you do alone. A3 task 2 asks for the same on the branch’s loads. We’ve seen this cost recipe on the D3 redesign slide (steps 3-5).

Step 1: where do you get each piece of information?
A team runs the same report queries on Athena every day and asks whether to move them to Trino on an EMR cluster.

## Where do you get each piece of information for this decision? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Data scanned by each report query :: Athena query history
  > Athena records each query's Data scanned. For billing, AWS rounds it up to the next MB, with a 10 MB minimum per query; the billed amount per run × price per TB × runs a day is Athena's daily cost, as in step 3.
- Expected report load next year: runs per day and the most runs in one hour :: Stakeholders and business case
  > The people who use the report know how often they will run it. Runs per day multiply Athena's daily cost, and the busiest hour decides how much cluster capacity is needed. How often it ran in the past is in Athena query history.
- Run time of one report on a cluster :: Pilot run on a cluster
  > Run time on the cluster you are considering tells you how many reports its nodes can serve in the hours it is up.
- Cluster's resource ceiling for your report (the most runs an hour it can keep up with) :: Pilot run on a cluster
  > Running reports in parallel on the pilot cluster shows how many runs an hour its nodes can finish; compare that ceiling with the busiest hour's load.
- Price per TB of Data scanned :: AWS price list
  > With Data scanned per run and runs a day, it gives Athena's daily cost, for your Region.
- Price per hour of each node :: AWS price list
  > EC2 price plus EMR price for the node type, times the number of nodes and the hours they are up, gives the cluster's daily cost; each node is billed per second while it is up, with a one-minute minimum.
- Budget for running the reports :: Stakeholders and business case
  > The crossover says which option is cheaper; the budget says whether that option is affordable.
- How soon after a request an answer is needed :: Stakeholders and business case
  > A cluster started on demand makes the first report wait while it starts; a cluster kept up for quick answers is billed while it waits.
- Who would look after a cluster :: Stakeholders and business case
  > Auto-termination, software updates and failed nodes need someone's time, which belongs in the decision even though it is not on the bill.
- :: S3 storage bill
  > The tables stay in S3 whichever engine reads them, so storage is the same in both options and does not decide between them.



Step 2: which option bills each part of the cost?
Your pilot measured one report query: about 3 GB of Data scanned on Athena, about 10 seconds on a 3-node EMR cluster, and about 2 minutes as a Glue job (Glue version 5). Here “EMR cluster” means everything its nodes are billed for: the EC2 price and the EMR price.

## For each line, choose the option that bills it. Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Query's Data scanned, priced per TB :: Athena
    > With Parquet, filtering on the partition column and naming fewer columns lowers this charge, because both lower Data scanned (L11, D2).
- Minimum of 10 MB of Data scanned per query :: Athena
    > A query that scans less than the minimum is billed as if it scanned the minimum.
- DPUs you chose for the job, priced per DPU-hour and billed for every second the job runs :: Glue
    > More DPUs or a longer run raise this charge.
- Minimum of one minute for each job run :: Glue
    > A job that finishes in 30 seconds is billed for 60; the minimum is per job run.
- Each node, priced per hour and billed per second while it is up, with a one-minute minimum, whether it is running a query or not :: EMR cluster
    > A node is charged while it runs, including when no query is using it.
- EMR price added to each node's EC2 price :: EMR cluster
    > EC2 supplies the instances and EMR manages the cluster, so both prices apply to every node.
- Storing the tables' files :: S3
    > Storage is billed by the bucket's service, the same whichever engine reads the files.
- Requests an engine makes to read the files :: S3
    > Reading files means requests to the bucket, billed at standard S3 rates on top of the engine's own bill.
- :: None of them
    > Every line here is billed by Athena, Glue, the EMR cluster or S3.

text:
What the table records

What does $snapshots show after each statement?
You copy the shop’s orders into your own Iceberg table, shop.orders_copy, with Athena, and run the statements below one after another. After each one you look at "orders_copy$snapshots".
D1, D4 and D5 checks might help you to answer. If it is still not super clear, experiment with the Tutorial 1 dataset.

---

---

## What does `$snapshots` show after each statement? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `CREATE TABLE shop.orders_copy ... AS SELECT` :: append
  > The copy adds data files and removes none, so the first snapshot is an append.
- `INSERT INTO shop.orders_copy` with the same hour of orders, run a second time :: append
  > A second run adds the same rows again as new data files: another append. It adds as many rows as the first run, so the table now holds duplicate rows.
- `DELETE FROM shop.orders_copy WHERE status = 'test'` (the table has a `status` column and some test orders) :: overwrite
  > Athena's `DELETE` writes delete files against existing data files, and Athena records it as overwrite.
- `OPTIMIZE shop.orders_copy REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK`, when enough small data files or delete files are eligible for a rewrite :: replace
  > Compaction adds and removes data files without changing the rows, which is what replace records.
- `ALTER TABLE shop.orders_copy ADD COLUMNS (gift_wrap boolean)` :: no new snapshot
  > A schema change writes a new metadata file; the list of snapshots stays as it was.
- `VACUUM shop.orders_copy` :: no new snapshot
  > `VACUUM` adds no snapshot. It removes only snapshots older than the table's age property (5 days by default), so in this sequence of statements run minutes apart it removes none.
- :: delete
  > The Iceberg spec has a delete operation, but Athena records its `DELETE` and `MERGE` as overwrite. Other engines may record delete.

  > Every query reads them, so every query would incur the fee per GB read. The files are small, so their storage cost is low.
- Last quarter's orders, kept for years, which customer service must query immediately, without waiting for a restore; each month, queries read 0.6 GB for each GB stored :: Standard-IA

  > Per GB stored, each year: Standard 12 × \$0.025 = \$0.30; Standard-IA 12 × \$0.0138 + \$0.01 ≈ \$0.176; Glacier Instant Retrieval 12 × \$0.005 + \$0.03 = \$0.09. The lowest price that Athena still reads directly; the higher fee per GB read hardly matters at one full read a year.
- Monthly exports of the product catalogue, kept seven years for tax rules, read in full once a year, and needed immediately when asked, without waiting for a restore :: Glacier Instant Retrieval
  > Kept for years, read in full once a year, and needed immediately: Glacier Instant Retrieval makes the file available immediately when it is read; no restore is required.
- :: Glacier Flexible Retrieval
  > A file in this class must be restored before it can be read, which takes minutes to hours, and an Athena query on an Iceberg table that holds such a file fails.

title: L11 review: assembling the lakehouse in Athena and Glue
text:
Terms used on this page

D1 catalog and table format
CTAS (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT). Writes a query’s result as a new table.
UNLOAD. Runs a query and writes its result as files to an empty S3 location, with no table.
ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS. A schema change, written as a new metadata file with no new snapshot.
Metadata tables ("t$partitions", "t$files", "t$snapshots", "t$history"). Read-only tables Athena makes from an Iceberg table’s metadata, one row per partition, data file or snapshot.
Snapshot operation. What $snapshots records for each snapshot: append (files added), overwrite (rows deleted or changed), replace (files rewritten, rows unchanged).
Field id. The number Iceberg gives a column when it is added. column_sizes in $files is keyed by it.


D2 layout
Partition spec. A source column and a transform, such as months(pickup_datetime); Iceberg derives each file’s partition value from it.
Sort order (WRITE ORDERED BY). The order Iceberg asks writers to sort rows in within each file, so each row group covers a narrow range.
Row-group size (write.parquet.row-group-size-bytes). The size at which the Parquet writer starts a new row group.
Projection pushdown. The engine hands the reader the query’s columns, so the others are never read.


D3 query engine
DPU-seconds. What a Glue run is billed for, DPUs × seconds of run time with a 1-minute minimum, at the DPU-hour price.
Data scanned limit. A per-query limit on an Athena workgroup. A query that passes it is cancelled and billed for the Data scanned before it stopped.


D4 corrections
Delete file. A file that lists rows removed from a data file. Readers skip those rows, and the data file stays as written.
MERGE. One statement that updates the rows whose key matches a source row and inserts the rest.


D5 upkeep
OPTIMIZE ... REWRITE DATA USING BIN_PACK. Compaction in Athena: rewrites small files into larger ones, recorded as a replace snapshot.
VACUUM. Expires snapshots older than the table’s age property, then deletes the files no remaining snapshot lists. Expired snapshots cannot be read.
Table property. A setting kept in the table’s metadata file, such as vacuum_max_snapshot_age_seconds.


D6 object storage
Storage class. S3’s price tier for an object: lower monthly price, a fee per GB read and a minimum duration.
Lifecycle rule. An S3 bucket rule that moves or deletes the objects under a prefix a set number of days after they were written.


Lake and lakehouse
Data lake. Raw files in object storage, read by engines that list the folders; a folder of files has no commit, no record of its schema and no history.
Lakehouse. A lake whose tables have a table format and a catalog, so readers see whole commits.
Query engine. Parses SQL, plans it and runs it: Spark SQL, Trino, DuckDB, Athena.
Catalog. Lists tables and points to each table’s current metadata file: the Glue Data Catalog.
Table format. Metadata files that say which data files are the table now, with the schema and the snapshots: Iceberg.
Object storage. Keeps files as objects in buckets: S3. Which files form a table is recorded in the metadata above it.
Storage format (file format). Encodes rows in one data file, with a footer: Parquet.


Iceberg’s levels
Catalog entry. The table’s name and the path of its current metadata file.
Metadata file. The schema, the partition spec (how files are grouped, for example by month) and the snapshots; each snapshot names a manifest list.
Manifest. Lists data files, each with its partition value, row count, and minimum and maximum per column.
Data file. A file that contains rows of a table: a Parquet file.
Commit. Writing new metadata files, then switching the catalog entry to the new one in one step; readers see the old snapshot or the new one, never half.
Snapshot. One version of the table: the data files that were the table after one commit.


What the table format fixes
Iceberg partitioning. The table is partitioned by a value Iceberg derives from a column, for example the month of pickup_datetime, and each data file’s partition value is kept in the manifests. Because the value is derived (hidden partitioning), a filter on the column itself skips files, with no folder partition column to name. Separately, the manifests keep each file’s minimum and maximum per column, which also let an engine skip files.
Delete file. A small file that lists which rows of a data file are deleted. Readers skip those rows, and the data file itself is not changed.
Compaction. Rewriting many small data files into fewer larger ones (OPTIMIZE).
Time travel. Reading the table as it was at an earlier snapshot, as long as that snapshot has not been expired.


Not layers of a lakehouse
Cluster manager. Starts an engine’s processes on a cluster’s nodes, for example YARN starting Spark’s executors on EMR (L5).
Connector. In Trino, how the engine reads one source, such as the Glue Data Catalog or a database (L10).
_SUCCESS file. An empty file Spark writes when a job finishes writing a folder; readers of the folder do not check it by default.
Folder partition column. A column whose value is a folder name, such as month=2024-03; a data lake skips folders only when a query names it.

text:
EC2: renting an instance

Setting up an instance for the harvest records *
A vineyard’s analysts keep their 2025 harvest records as Parquet files in the S3 bucket vineyard-harvest. They launch one EC2 instance to run a FastAPI service that answers questions about the harvest, with these requirements.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which launch setting meets each requirement? Not all options will be used.

- The service needs 8 vCPUs and 32 GiB of memory. :: instance type
    > The type fixes vCPUs, memory and network performance: an m6a.2xlarge has 8 vCPUs and 32 GiB. You pick the instance type from a menu; you cannot choose the vCPUs, memory and network performance separately.
- The instance starts from the image the analysts saved last season, with Amazon Linux and their Python packages already installed before the first boot. :: image (AMI)
    > An image (AMI) holds the operating system and the software an instance starts from, and you can make your own. A user data script could install the same packages, but only on the first boot, after the instance has started; here the packages are already in the saved image when the instance starts.
- The service's code is downloaded and started on the first boot, without anyone logging in. :: user data
    > User data is a script passed at launch that runs once, on the instance's first start.
- Anyone on the internet can reach the service on port 8000, and no other port is open. :: security group
    > A security group opens a port to the addresses you name; every other port stays closed.
- 60 GB of downloaded weather files must still be there after the instance is stopped and started again. :: EBS volume
    > An EBS volume is a disk attached to the instance over the network, as its main disk or an extra one, and its data survives a stop and start of the instance.
- :: Elastic IP
    > An Elastic IP is an address held for you that stays the same across a stop and start. An Elastic IP sets where the instance can be reached; it does not control which ports are open, and it does not store files.
- :: IAM role
    > A role is the instance's identity when it calls AWS, such as reading the bucket. A role controls what the instance may do; it does not control who can reach the instance's ports.
- :: Lambda layer
    > A layer packages libraries for a Lambda function. An instance gets its software from its image or from a script it runs at first boot.

Slide: 25, 29, 30 (also 18, 27, 38)


Who is responsible for each task, on an instance and on a function?
A team runs the same daily harvest report two ways: on an EC2 instance, a t3a.large running a FastAPI service, and as a Lambda function with a pandas layer and an execution role that can read the bucket vineyard-harvest. These tasks come up over one month.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each task, who is responsible for it on the instance and on the function? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- Choosing how much memory the report runs with. :: you on both
    > On the instance you pick the instance type, and the type fixes the memory together with the vCPUs. On the function you pick one memory setting, and CPU follows that setting. The memory setting fixes the size of each execution environment and is your responsibility; AWS is responsible for the number of execution environments.
- Restarting the service after it crashes. :: you on the instance, AWS on the function
    > On the instance, you run the service, so restarting the service after a crash is your responsibility. On Lambda, AWS is responsible for the execution environment, and the next call runs the function again.
- Picking the storage class of the objects in `vineyard-harvest`. :: you on both
    > The report reads the same S3 bucket on the instance and on the function, and you are responsible for choosing the storage class of the objects in the bucket.
- Starting Python and the program that answers requests. :: you on the instance, AWS on the function
    > On the instance the runtime and the web server (uvicorn for FastAPI) are your responsibility to install and start. On Lambda you supply only the function, and AWS is responsible for starting the runtime.
- Shutting the compute down when the day's reports are done. :: you on the instance, AWS on the function
    > The instance keeps running until you stop it, and you pay for that time. A function runs only while it is called, and AWS is responsible for what happens between calls.
- Adding capacity when 200 analysts ask for the report in the same minute. :: you on the instance, AWS on the function
    > The instance has the capacity of the type you picked, and adding more is your responsibility. On Lambda, scaling to many calls at once is AWS's responsibility.
- :: AWS on both
    > AWS is responsible for the hardware and the hypervisor beneath an EC2 instance. The tasks listed here remain your responsibility on the instance.
- :: AWS on the instance, you on the function
    > This option reverses who is responsible on the instance and on the function. On the instance, AWS is responsible only for the hardware and the virtual machine; you are responsible for the capacity (the type, starting and stopping the instance), the operating system, the runtime, the libraries, the code, the permissions and the security group. On the function, you choose the memory setting, and AWS is responsible for the number of execution environments, the operating system and the runtime.

section: Lambda: a function that runs only when called
text:
Lambda: a function that runs only when called

Cold starts, warm calls and the memory setting
A Lambda function returns a crop-yield estimate for one field. An execution environment is the isolated space Lambda sets up to run a function, with its memory and a temporary disk; it handles one call at a time and may be reused for later calls. Before its handler runs, the function loads a 60 MB table of soil data from S3 and keeps it in memory. A new version was deployed at 08:55. A call that uses an execution environment that already exists takes about 80 ms; a call that needs a new one takes about 3 s, most of it to load the table. For this question, assume no execution environment exists for the new version before the 09:00 call, that Lambda reuses an idle execution environment when one is available, and that it removes environments that remain idle overnight. These calls arrive:
09:00:00            the first call of the day
09:00:20            after the 09:00:00 call finished, nothing else running
09:00:20 + 50 ms    while the 09:00:20 call is still running
09:00:40            both execution environments idle
07:30 next morning  the first call after no calls all night

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each call, which execution environment does Lambda run it in? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- the call at 09:00:00 :: new execution environment
    > The 09:00:00 call has a cold start because no execution environment exists yet for the version deployed at 08:55. Lambda creates a new environment and loads the 60 MB table into it before the handler runs, so the call takes about 3 s.
- the call at 09:00:20 :: existing execution environment
    > The 09:00:20 call is warm: Lambda reuses an existing execution environment. The environment from 09:00:00 is idle, with its soil table still in memory.
- the call 50 ms after 09:00:20 :: new execution environment
    > The call 50 ms after 09:00:20 has a cold start because the environment handling the 09:00:20 call is still busy. Lambda creates a new environment and loads the 60 MB table into it before the handler runs, so the call takes about 3 s.
- the call at 09:00:40 :: existing execution environment
    > The 09:00:40 call is warm because both execution environments are idle then. Lambda uses one of them and reuses its loaded table.
- the call at 07:30 the next morning :: new execution environment
    > The 07:30 call the next morning has a cold start because Lambda has removed the environments that remained idle overnight. Lambda creates a new environment and loads the 60 MB table into it before the handler runs, so the call takes about 3 s.
- :: new EC2 instance
    > Lambda does not start an instance for you. In its standard mode, Lambda creates execution environments on hardware AWS operates, and you never see or pick an instance.
- :: existing execution environment, soil table loaded again
    > An existing execution environment retains the soil table in memory, so a warm call does not repeat the start-up load. Reusing the execution environment explains why the call takes about 80 ms instead of 3 s.

A Lambda function set to 512 MB of memory reads a 40 MB CSV file of field readings and groups it with pandas, which comes from a layer. Each call uses about 300 MB of memory and takes 8 s, with its CPU busy the whole time. The timeout is 30 s.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which change is likely to make each call finish sooner?

1. [x] Raise the memory setting to 1,769 MB
    > Lambda's CPU follows the memory setting: 1,769 MB gives one full vCPU, and 512 MB gives less than a third of one vCPU. The CPU is busy for the whole 8 s, so compute is the bottleneck; more memory gives more CPU, and the call finishes sooner, although 300 MB is enough to hold the data.
1. [ ] Pick an instance type with more CPU for the function
    > This option treats the function as an EC2 instance. A function has no instance type to choose: you pick a memory setting, and CPU follows that setting.
1. [ ] Raise the timeout from 30 s to 60 s
    > The timeout is the longest a call may run before Lambda stops it. The calls finish in 8 s, well inside 30 s, and a higher limit does not make them faster.

title: L2 review: EC2, S3 and Lambda by example
text:
Terms used on this page
From the course flashcards, grouped by topic. Practise them in quiz mode, or try the match game.

EC2 instances
Instance. A virtual machine you rent from AWS, billed per second for the time it runs. Stopping it ends the compute charge, but its EBS disk still bills.
Instance type. The size you pick when you launch an EC2 server: how many vCPUs and how much memory it has, how fast its network is, and whether it has its own local disk.
EBS volume. A disk an EC2 instance reaches over the network, as its main disk or an extra one. Its data survives a stop, and it bills per GB-month while it exists, even when the instance is stopped.
Security group. The rules that say what network traffic may reach an EC2 instance and what it may send out, by protocol, port and address. They do not decide what the instance may do with other AWS resources.
IAM policy. A JSON document that says which actions are allowed on which AWS resources. Attached to a role, it sets what anything using that role may do.


S3
S3. AWS’s object store. You reach each object over the network by its name inside a bucket, and the data stays with no server running.
Bucket. A named container in S3 that holds objects. Its name is part of every object’s address.
Object key. The full name of one stored file inside an S3 bucket. It is only a name, unrelated to the column a group-by or a join uses.
Prefix. The leading part of an object’s name, such as day=2012-06-14/. S3 lists objects by it, and the console’s folders are built from it; the general-purpose buckets we use have no real folders.


Lambda functions
Lambda function. The unit you deploy to AWS Lambda: your code and its settings, run each time a trigger fires. One setting, memory, also sets its CPU and its price per millisecond.
Execution role. The identity AWS takes on when it runs a Lambda function. It decides which resources the code may read or change.
Execution environment. The isolated space AWS sets up to run a Lambda function, with its memory and a temporary disk. AWS may reuse it for later calls and pauses it between them.
Cold start. The set-up before the first call in a new Lambda environment: AWS loads the code, then your code’s initialisation runs, such as opening connections and importing libraries.
Handler. The function in your code that Lambda calls on each invocation, taking event and context. Code outside it runs once per environment, so a client built there is reused.


Billing
Time shape of demand. When a workload asks for its resources across a day or a week: a steady rate, a daily rhythm, a burst, or a scheduled job. With the peak rate, it decides whether provisioned or usage-based billing is cheaper.
Provisioned capacity. Compute you pay for while it is allocated to you, used or not. Unlike pay-per-use compute, its charge continues when nothing runs.
Usage-based billing. Charges for measured work, such as each request or each millisecond a function runs. They stop when nothing runs; stored data and logs still cost money.
Idle test. The question to ask of each compute charge: does it bill while nothing runs? If yes, it is provisioned capacity. Storage and logs are counted separately.

text:
Storage side of scaling up

What does each filter condition make Spark read?
A city library keeps its loan records for September to December 2025 in S3 as Parquet, one folder partition per month of loan_date:
s3://city-library/loans/
├── month=2025-09/
│   └── part-0.parquet        about 150 MB
├── month=2025-10/
│   └── part-0.parquet
├── month=2025-11/
│   └── part-0.parquet
└── month=2025-12/
    └── part-0.parquet
Each file holds only its month’s loans, in many row groups (the blocks of rows inside a Parquet file). Inside a file the rows are sorted by branch_id (the library has 40 branches); the loan_days column is in no particular order, and every row group has some loans longer than 21 days. Spark on an EMR cluster runs queries that each have one filter condition, and each condition matches some loans. Assume the reader rules out row groups only by their min and max.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## For each filter condition on the loans folder, what does Spark open and read? Each option may be used once, more than once, or not at all.

- `month = '2025-11'` :: 1 or 2 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition names the folder partition key, so Spark opens the November 2025 folder and rules out the other 3 by their names, without reading their row groups. Every row in the November 2025 file is a November 2025 loan, so every row group is read.
- `month IN ('2025-11', '2025-12')` :: 1 or 2 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition names the folder partition key, so Spark opens the November 2025 and December 2025 folders and rules out the other 2 by their names, without reading their row groups. Every row in those two files is a November 2025 or December 2025 loan, so every row group of both is read.
- `branch_id = 17` :: all 4 files opened, some row groups may be skipped
    > All 4 files are opened, because the condition does not name `month`. Inside each file the rows are sorted by branch, so each row group has a narrow `branch_id` range. Where the writer stored each row group's min and max in the footer, the reader skips the row groups whose range does not include 17, without fetching those row groups.
- `loan_days > 21` :: all 4 files opened, every row group read
    > The condition does not name `month`, so Spark opens all 4 files. Every row group has some loans longer than 21 days, so each row group's maximum `loan_days` is above 21 and the footer rules none out. Without a sort, values usually spread like this, but not always: a row group whose maximum happened to be 21 or less would be skipped.
- :: footers read, no row group read
    > A footer records where the row groups are and each row group's min and max; the footer holds no rows. Footers alone answer a query only when their min and max rule out every row group. Each condition here leaves at least one row group to read: the `month` conditions name folders that hold loans, and each of the other conditions matches some loans, so at least one row group holds a matching row and has to be read.

Slide: 15, 20, 21, 23, 31


Which folder partition key best supports the analysts’ one-day and one-month queries?
A news site keeps its page views from January 2024 to December 2025 in S3 as one Parquet file, with no folder partitions:
s3://news-site/page-views/
└── page-views.parquet    4 GB, rows sorted by view time, many row groups
The analysts query the file with DuckDB. Their common queries filter on the view time, one day or one month, and count views per article category. The team will rewrite the file into folder partitions on one key, and the analysts will write each time filter so that it also names that key. The rewrite keeps the rows sorted by view time, with many row groups in each file. DuckDB recommends at least 100 MB per folder partition.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which folder partition key best supports the analysts' one-day and one-month queries?

1. [x] `month`: 24 folders of about 170 MB
    > Each query names one month, so it opens one folder. Inside that folder, the footer's minimum and maximum view times let a daily query skip other days' row groups, and each folder partition is over 100 MB. A `day` key would also let a daily query open one folder, but each folder would hold only about 5.5 MB, below DuckDB's 100 MB guidance, and a monthly query would open about 30 of them.
1. [ ] `day`: 731 folders of about 5.5 MB
    > The `day` key matches the daily filter, but each 5.5 MB folder partition is below the 100 MB guidance. A monthly query opens about 30 small folder partitions, one per day of the month, while sorting by view time already lets a daily query skip row groups within a monthly folder partition.
1. [ ] `category`: 12 folders of about 330 MB
    > The queries group by category and filter on dates. Every query needs all 12 categories, so it opens all 12 folders and the key rules nothing out.

Slide: 22–23


Which changes spread the scan over all four threads?
A hotel chain exports its 2025 bookings as one Parquet file:
bookings-2025.parquet     1.2 GB, 30 million rows, one row group
About 2.5 million of the rows are July 2025 bookings. DuckDB with four threads on an m6a.xlarge (4 vCPU, 16 GiB) computes the average nightly price per hotel for July 2025 in 3 s. During the query one vCPU is busy and three stay idle. Every rewrite below writes row groups of about 100,000 rows unless the option says otherwise.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which of these changes let the July query finish sooner by spreading its scan over all four threads? Select every change that does.

- [x] Rewrite the file with row groups of about 100,000 rows
    > At about 100,000 rows each, the 30 million rows make about 300 row groups. DuckDB gives each thread whole row groups to read, so the four threads share the scan.
- [x] Rewrite the bookings file as folder partitions by month, one file per month
    > At about 100,000 rows per row group, the 2.5 million July 2025 rows make about 25 row groups in the July 2025 file. DuckDB gives each thread whole row groups to read, so the four threads share the scan. The query opens only the July 2025 file when its filter names the `month` key; with a filter on the booking date alone, DuckDB opens all twelve files, and their footers rule out the other months' row groups.
- [ ] Rewrite the bookings file as one Parquet file sorted by hotel, still one row group
    > The file has one row group, so one thread reads it and the other three have nothing to read. Sorting changes which rows sit next to each other inside the row group; the file still has one row group for DuckDB to give its threads.
- [ ] Set DuckDB to 32 threads
    > The file has one row group, so one thread reads it and the extra threads have nothing to read. The instance has only 4 vCPUs to run the threads.
- [ ] Move to an m6a.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB)
    > The file has one row group, so one thread reads it and the extra vCPUs have nothing to read. More memory does not increase the number of row groups.

text:
Scaling out: more nodes, and a network between them

Which first change cuts the daily query’s time most?
A parcel company keeps three years of parcel scans as CSV in S3:
s3://parcel-co/scans/
├── part-0.csv
│   …
└── part-N.csv            450 GB in all, 25 columns, 2023 to 2025
A query that runs every day counts late parcels per depot for one month and reads 3 of the 25 columns. On one m6a.xlarge it takes 50 minutes. The instance reads from S3 above its baseline network rate only for the first minutes; for most of the 50 minutes it reads at the m6a.xlarge’s baseline of 1.56 Gbps, about 195 MB/s, and reading all 450 GB at that rate takes about 38 minutes.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which first change is likely to cut the daily query's time most?

1. [x] Convert the CSV once to Parquet
    > The query then fetches only 3 of the 25 columns, compressed and stored as typed values, so most of the 450 GB is not sent over the network. With its data converted to Parquet, L1's taxi query went from 14 min to 5.5 s on one instance. Three nodes cut the time to about a third at best, while reading 3 of 25 columns already cuts the data fetched to about an eighth, before compression, so the Parquet change cuts more.
1. [ ] Run the query on EMR with three m6a.xlarge core nodes
    > Three m6a.xlarge nodes have about three times the network capacity of one, so the query takes at best about a third of the time, and the three nodes still read every byte of the CSV.
1. [ ] Split the CSV into many smaller files
    > Smaller files hold the same 450 GB in total, and every byte is still read over the same network.

Slide: 3, 24, 30, L2 18


Which node type should the team add for this job? *
An EMR cluster with one primary node and two core nodes runs a long Spark job that reads its input from S3 and writes its results back to S3. To finish the job sooner, the team wants to add nodes for it and remove them soon afterwards, without losing any data the cluster stores.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## Which node type should the team add for this job?

1. [x] Task nodes
    > Task nodes run executors and store no HDFS blocks, so they can be removed as soon as the job ends; the input and the results stay in S3.
1. [ ] Core nodes
    > Core nodes run executors and store HDFS blocks, which exist only on the cluster, so removing a core node risks losing those blocks. The team should not add core nodes for one job and remove them afterwards.
1. [ ] Larger primary node
    > The primary node manages the cluster and coordinates its services. The job's parallel work runs in executors on the core and task nodes, so enlarging the primary adds no capacity for that work.

Slide: 29, L5 18


After how many queries has the rewrite paid back? *
Vancouver publishes its Van311 non-emergency service requests as open data. A team keeps five years of them in S3 as one CSV file per year, and a weekly query reads them all:
s3://van-311/requests/
├── 2021.csv
│   …
└── 2025.csv
Rewriting the CSV files once as sorted Parquet in folder partitions uses 1,200 CPU-seconds. The weekly query uses 50 CPU-seconds on the CSV and 10 CPU-seconds on the rewritten files.

---
shuffle_answers: true
---

## After how many weekly queries has the rewrite paid back its CPU-seconds?

1. [x] 30 queries
    > Each query saves 50 − 10 = 40 CPU-seconds, and 1,200 / 40 = 30 weekly runs.
1. [ ] 24 queries
    > 1,200 / 50 divides by what the old query cost. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 40 CPU-seconds.
1. [ ] 120 queries
    > 1,200 / 10 divides by what the new query costs. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 40 CPU-seconds.
1. [ ] 20 queries
    > 1,200 / (50 + 10) adds the two costs together. The rewrite is paid back by what each query saves, 50 − 10 = 40 CPU-seconds.

Slide: 32
